title: The role of age and self-control in shaping prosocial behavior: Age and preschool attendance as moderators
abstract: Background: The development of self-control in early childhood is crucial for fostering prosocial behaviors such as helping, sharing, and comforting. This study explores the relationship between self-control and prosocial behavior in preschool children, considering the influence of age and preschool attendance. Objective: To investigate how age and preschool attendance moderate the relationship between self-control and prosocial behaviors in young children. Participants and Setting: A sample of 97 preschoolers aged 36 to 72 months was assessed using the Social Behavior Assessment System for Preschool and the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test-Revised. Methods: The study employed path analysis to examine the direct effects of age on self-control and prosocial behaviors, and the moderating role of preschool attendance in these relationships. Results: The findings indicate that age positively influences both self-control and prosocial behaviors. Additionally, preschool attendance significantly moderates the relationship between self-control and prosocial behavior, with children attending preschool demonstrating higher levels of both traits. The effect sizes for the relationships were statistically significant, with a path coefficient of .41 for age's influence on self-control and .38 for self-control's impact on prosocial behavior (p < .001). Conclusions: Enhancing self-control in preschool settings can significantly boost prosocial behaviors in children. These findings underscore the importance of early childhood education in promoting social and emotional development.

title: Out-earning or outnumbering: Two routes to cooperation in the fixed-role trust game on structured populations
abstract: Trust underlies cooperation, but sustaining it is individually costly and difficult under rational self-interest. In the trust game, a trustor invests part of an endowment and a trustee returns a share of the multiplied proceeds. Under fixed roles on a square lattice, agents play only with orthogonal neighbors of opposite-roles, but mimic diagonal neighbors of the same-role, decoupling interaction from imitation networks. Trust that collapses in well-mixed populations can instead co-evolve with trustworthiness on the lattice within a narrow range of the return parameter under strong selection. Comparing update rules uncovers two distinct routes to cooperation. First, pairwise imitation depends on reciprocators (that is, reciprocating trustees) outperforming betrayers through local assortment, forming clusters of trustworthy trustees around generous trustors. In contrast, a neighborhood rule allows the local majority of reciprocators convert an isolated betrayer regardless of the payoff, outnumbering betrayers rather than out-earning them. This collective-recruitment route sustains trust-reciprocate interactions over a wider range of the return parameter. The two routes differ, however, in what they require: pairwise spread needs only cross-role assortment and still produces cooperation on a geometry-free degree-regular network, whereas collective recruitment does not survive that change. Degree heterogeneity adds no route of its own, and whether it leaves cooperation standing depends on which role carries it and on how payoffs are aggregated. Of the structures examined here, only the lattice supports both routes.

title: Interactive Effects of Risk Propensity and Secure Attachment on Prosocial Risk-Taking: Based on Polynomial Regression and Response Surface Analysis
abstract: Abstract Prosocial risk-taking behavior refers to voluntary actions that benefit others despite potential personal costs. Despite its importance, the interactive effects of personality traits such as risk propensity and secure attachment on prosocial risk-taking behavior remain underexplored. This study investigated these effects and the mediating roles of risk perception and outcome expectancy among 762 Chinese undergraduates. Participants completed validated scales assessing the variables. Response surface analysis revealed significant congruence effects, indicating higher prosocial risk-taking behavior when both traits are high. While the levels of these traits are incongruent, individuals with low risk propensity and high secure attachment exhibit more prosocial risk-taking behavior compared to those with high risk propensity and low secure attachment, which reflects secure attachment's compensatory role in low risk propensity scenarios. Outcome expectancy partially mediated the interaction, but risk perception did not. These findings clarify the interactive mechanisms of dual personality traits in prosocial risk-taking behavior and provide a theoretical basis for encouraging individuals to engage more in such behaviors.

title: Structural differentiation and collaborative optimization of the spatial network of pension care service in megacity behemoths: a case study of Guangzhou, China.
abstract: Against the backdrop of population aging, cross-district coordination and equitable allocation of pension care resources have become increasingly important for improving service accessibility and urban governance in megacities. This study examines spatial disparities and interdistrict connections in pension care services across Guangzhou's 11 districts, focusing on resource distribution, transportation accessibility, and network structure. A multidimensional evaluation framework encompassing institutional care capacity, home- and community-based care capacity, and medical support capacity for pension care was developed. The entropy weighting method was employed to evaluate the comprehensive development level of pension care services in each district. An interdistrict transport impedance index was constructed based on public transportation travel times, and a modified gravity model was applied to estimate the strength of interdistrict connections in pension care services. Social network analysis was subsequently conducted to examine network density, centrality, and core-periphery structures. The findings reveal substantial spatial disparities and functional differentiation in pension care services across Guangzhou. Transportation accessibility generally decreases from central to peripheral districts. The interdistrict service network exhibits a centralized and hierarchical structure, with Baiyun and Tianhe occupying prominent positions in network connectivity. Liwan, Tianhe, and Baiyun constitute the network's core area, whereas peripheral districts demonstrate relatively weak interdistrict connections and insufficient coordination. The findings underscore the need to strengthen cross-district coordination and address spatial inequalities in pension care services. Policy priorities include enhancing resource integration and service coordination among core districts, developing secondary pension care service centers, and improving mechanisms for resource sharing, service referral, and digital collaboration in peripheral districts. These measures could contribute to a more balanced, multi-tiered, and interconnected urban pension care service network.

title: Minority control maximizes cumulative cooperation
abstract: Abstract Designing incentives that promote cooperation is a central problem in public policy. Such incentives are typically evaluated by the stable cooperation level, which implicitly assumes that they last forever. In practice, incentives are costly and must end, after which the cooperation they built may erode. Since cooperation counts for as long as it lasts, a more practically relevant question is how to spend a limited budget to maximize the cooperation accumulated over the evolutionary process. Here, we develop a framework for maximizing cumulative cooperation in evolving populations through rewards or punishments. For general social dilemmas, including the prisoner’s dilemma, snowdrift game, and stag-hunt game, we show that reaching a target state at minimum cumulative cost follows a minority-control principle: reward minority cooperators or punish minority defectors. Furthermore, under a fixed control budget, to maximize the cumulative cooperation, the optimal strategy is to apply this principle to drive the population to a desired state, then maintain that state until the budget is exhausted, and finally allow natural evolution. Our results shift the focus from maximizing cooperation at a single time point to maximizing cooperation accumulated over time.

title: Later life precarity and longitudinal frailty trajectories in older adults.
abstract: The concept of precarity is increasingly being applied in social gerontology to understand risks and uncertainties faced by older adults. However, existing research has not captured precarity quantitatively nor has it modelled its effect on older adults' health. We therefore develop a Later Life Precarity Index and model its association with frailty. Using longitudinal data on 15,733 older adults from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, we examine the association between frailty and risks across the domains of finances, pensions, employment, housing, relationship and unpaid care-giving. We then develop the Later Life Precarity Index and model its longitudinal association with a Frailty Index using hybrid panel regression. The results indicate that multiple social risks are strongly and independently associated with frailty, particularly around finances, housing, fuel poverty and food insecurity. In longitudinal models, the precarity index explains both between-individual differences and within-individual changes in frailty and performs substantially better than standard measures of socio-economic status (wealth and education). The strong longitudinal association of the precarity index with frailty suggests that social gerontology's growing focus on precarity is a useful lens for understanding the diverse, changing and new forms of social risk that impact frailty. By developing, testing and sharing this novel measure of later life precarity, this study brings potential for new understandings of the evolving drivers of inequalities in the health of older adults.

title: Sex-specific associations between polygenic scores for major psychiatric conditions and social communication difficulties in the general population: Deeper insights from the UK ALSPAC study.
abstract: Social communication difficulties are a transdiagnostic feature of many psychiatric conditions and show genetic overlap with multiple psychiatric conditions in the general population. While marked sex differences exist in both social communication difficulties and in the prevalence of psychiatric conditions, it remains underinvestigated whether these differences extend to genetic associations. We therefore investigated sex-specific patterns of genetic sharing between autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), schizophrenia, depression, anxiety, and bipolar disorder and social communication difficulties across development in the general population. Using data from the UK ALSPAC cohort (n ≤ 8795), we examined associations between polygenic scores for each condition and parent-reported social communication difficulties (Social Communication Disorder Checklist) at ages 7, 10, 13, and 16, including sex interactions. Boys had more social communication difficulties than girls up to age 13, whereas polygenic scores did not differ by sex. title: Language and economic decisions
abstract: Many economic problems are framed using language. We introduce a language-based utility function to rationalize how linguistic framing shapes decision-making. We derive a prediction in the dictator game and empirically test it across 107 experimental instructions. Language is evaluated using deep learning and human methods: BERT, MoralBERT, GPT, and experimental subjects. Among these, GPT evaluations best predict giving behavior. We then examine the mechanism underlying this effect, showing that moral, rather than emotional, evaluations account for the observed patterns. Finally, we assess robustness by deriving predictions in equity–efficiency trade-off, ultimatum, and corruption games, and by showing that GPT evaluations predict human behavior also in these contexts. Our results show that language is a quantifiable dimension of economic decision-making.

title: Spyglass is a framework for reproducible and shareable neuroscience research.
abstract: Scientific progress depends on reliable and reproducible results. Progress can be accelerated when data are shared and re-analyzed to address new questions. Current approaches to storing and analyzing neural data involve bespoke formats and software that make replication and reuse of data difficult. To address these challenges, we created Spyglass, an open-source data management and analysis framework written in Python. Spyglass provides reproducible pipelines for common neuroscience analyses and sharing of raw data, intermediate analyses, and final results within and across labs. Spyglass uses the Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) standard and includes pipelines for spectral filtering, spike sorting, pose tracking, and neural decoding. Spyglass can be extended to apply existing and newly developed pipelines to datasets from multiple sources. We demonstrate these features in the context of a cross-laboratory replication by applying advanced state space decoding algorithms to publicly available data. New users can try out Spyglass on a Jupyter Hub hosted by HHMI and 2i2c: https://spyglass.hhmi.2i2c.cloud/.

title: Can peace radio shift social cohesion? Experimental evidence from a one-off narrative exposure in rural Sierra Leone
abstract: Conflicts between farmers and herders are a growing source of violence across West Africa, yet rigorous evidence on effective peacebuilding interventions in such settings remains limited. This paper examines whether a brief, one-off exposure to a peace-oriented radio narrative can shift intergroup attitudes and cooperative behaviour in Sierra Leone’s Falaba District, where farmer–herder tensions are recurrent. We embedded a randomised audio prime into a household survey of nearly 2,000 respondents, assigning participants to listen either to an eight-minute segment of a locally produced peace drama or to a placebo health narrative, and measured outcomes immediately afterwards. We find null average effects: the treatment produces no detectable changes in generalised trust or altruistic behaviour and only small, non-robust improvements in tolerance towards selected outgroups. Exploratory analyses find some variation in estimated effects by gender and tribal identity, though most subgroup patterns do not survive correction for multiple comparisons and are treated as suggestive rather than confirmed findings. The results overall suggest that brief narrative exposure is insufficient to shift intergroup attitudes on average, and that low-dose peace messaging should not be expected to substitute for sustained programming. Policy relevance. Our null average effects caution against expecting measurable impact from low-dose peace messaging without sustained engagement or complementary programming. The exploratory subgroup analyses further suggest that audience composition may matter: the same message may be received differently depending on listeners’ social position, reinforcing the importance of pre-testing content with diverse audience segments. These findings speak to efforts to build inclusive partnerships for sustainable peace (SDG 16 and 17) and to the growing policy interest in scalable, community-based approaches to farmer-herder conflict reduction across West Africa and the Sahel.

title: The Benefits of Prosociality towards AI Agents: Examining the Effects of Helping AI Agents on Human Well-Being
abstract: Prosocial behaviors, such as helping others, are well-known to enhance human well-being. While there is a growing trend of humans helping AI agents, it remains unclear whether the well-being benefits of helping others extend to interactions with non-human entities. To address this, we conducted an experiment (N = 295) to explore how helping AI agents impacts human well-being, especially when the agents fulfill human basic psychological needs--relatedness, competence, and autonomy--during the interaction. Our findings showed that helping AI agents reduced participants' feelings of loneliness. When AI met participants' needs for competence and autonomy during the helping process, there was a further decrease in loneliness and an increase in positive affect. However, when AI did not meet participants' need for relatedness, participants experienced an increase in positive affect. We discuss the implications of these findings for understanding how AI can support human well-being.

title: Cinematic narrative transportation and prosocial tendencies in college students: a moderated mediation model
abstract: Background Narrative-based entertainment has been associated with audience members’ values and behavioral tendencies, yet the mechanisms linking cinematic narrative experiences to prosocial tendencies remain unclear. Drawing on narrative transportation theory and character identification theory, this study examined whether character identification mediates the association between cinematic narrative transportation and prosocial tendencies among college students and whether moral identity moderates the second stage of this indirect pathway. Methods A cross-sectional film-viewing survey was conducted with 1054 Chinese undergraduates ( M = 20.64 ± 1.62 years; 60.06% female). After viewing Dying to Survive , participants completed the narrative engagement scale, character identification scale, moral identity scale and prosocial behavior measure(used to assess prosocial tendencies). PROCESS Models 4 and 14, with 5,000 bootstrap samples, were used to test the mediation and moderated mediation models. Results Narrative transportation was positively correlated with prosocial tendencies ( r = 0.67, p < 0.01). Character identification partially explained the association (indirect effect = 0.012, Boot 95% CI excluding zero;2.72% of the total effect). Moral identity moderated the character identification–prosocial tendencies pathway ( b = 0.106, p = 0.009): the association was significant at moderate and high levels of moral identity ( b = 0.090 and 0.139, respectively, p < 0.001), but not at a low level ( b = 0.013, p = 0.691). The conditional indirect effects followed the same pattern (moderate: indirect effect = 0.014, 95% Boot CI [0.007, 0.023]; high: indirect effect = 0.022, 95% Boot CI [0.011, 0.034]; index of moderated mediation = 0.017, 95% Boot CI [0.005, 0.031]). Conclusion Cinematic narrative transportation was associated with college students’ prosocial tendencies partly through character identification, with moral identity serving as a moderating factor in this process. Film-based aesthetic education featuring moral growth arcs may be related to prosocial tendencies, particularly among students with higher moral identity.

title: Duty and permission for utilitarians
abstract: Abstract In ethics, some reasons for action have more justifying force (tending to render an action permissible) than requiring force (tending to render an action obligatory). Notably, the fact that a socially beneficial action would entail significant self-sacrifice often provides one with a justification to refrain, without producing any requirement to refrain. At the same time, in similar circumstances, the fact that a socially beneficial action would require imposing significant sacrifices on others may produce a moral requirement to refrain. I offer a rule utilitarian account of this, according to which the recognition of justifying reasons to refrain from self-sacrifice functions as a kind of concession that an optimal system of social rules must make to human partiality to avoid widespread resistance and circumvention of the rules. In such a system, we also have justifications for sacrificing third parties for the sake of maximizing utility in just those situations in which a practice of so sacrificing third parties would create benign rather than perverse incentives. I go on to consider why there are limits to how low the demands of morality may be (for extremely selfish people), as well as limits to how much personal sacrifice one may make for the sake of others (for extremely altruistic people).

title: HSG-Net: A Scheduling-Aware Heterogeneous Graph Surrogate for Aviation Sensing-Data Processing Chains.
abstract: Efficient end-to-end timing evaluation is essential for the design and configuration of partitioned aviation sensing-data processing chains. Task activation, partition scheduling, message dependencies, and resource sharing jointly influence flow delay, while small variations in message arrival times may introduce substantial waiting across partition execution boundaries. Conventional reference simulation can capture these interactions but becomes computationally expensive when numerous candidate configurations must be evaluated. To address this challenge, this paper proposes HSG-Net, a scheduling-aware heterogeneous graph surrogate for predicting mean end-to-end delay from system configuration information. The proposed method represents tasks, partition windows, data flows, and hardware resources as interconnected entities, integrating explicit scheduling descriptors with heterogeneous relational dependencies. Graph message passing captures scheduling and resource interactions, while an adaptive direct-flow pathway preserves flow-local timing information and combines it with graph-derived representations for multi-scale delay prediction. On 7168 held-out test flows, the three-seed HSG-Net ensemble achieves a mean absolute error of 6.372 ms relative to reference-simulator labels, with 81.18% of predictions within a 10 ms absolute-error tolerance. Architectural comparisons demonstrate improved prediction over the evaluated direct-flow-only control, supporting the complementary use of relational context and flow-local information. Furthermore, HSG-Net also supports offline candidate screening through a validation-calibrated rule that allocates reference-simulation effort. The proposed approach provides an efficient, simulation-assisted method for timing evaluation and early-stage design-space exploration of partitioned aviation sensing-data processing architectures.

title: Within-family heritability estimates for behavioural and disease phenotypes from 500,000 sibling pairs of diverse ancestries.
abstract: Quantification of the direct effect of genetic variation on human behavioural traits is important for understanding between-individual variation in socioeconomic and health outcomes but estimates of their heritability can be biased by between-family indirect genetic effects. By contrast, using within-family variation in DNA sharing is robust to most confounding factors including shared environmental effects and population stratification. Yet, accurate estimates for most traits are not available using this design, and none for non-European ancestry populations. Here we analyse approximately 500,000 sibling pairs with diverse genetic ancestries and obtain within-family heritability estimates for 14 phenotypes, including two well-studied model traits: height (0.70 ± 0.03) and BMI (0.49 ± 0.03). For behaviour, we find significant within-family heritability for smoking initiation (0.34 ± 0.05), alcohol consumption (0.18 ± 0.04), number of children (0.27 ± 0.11) and personality ('talk versus listen', 0.48 ± 0.13). In addition, we estimated large heritability for type 2 diabetes (0.43 ± 0.06) and asthma (0.34 ± 0.06), whose risk factors include behavioural traits. Overall, we show concordant estimates across ancestry groups and highlight a significant contribution of shared environmental effects for behaviour and type 2 diabetes risk, which may have inflated between-family estimates. Altogether, our results provide within-family evidence that genetic variation is associated with variation in complex traits, common disease and exposures. Our heritability estimates are concordant across genetic ancestries, lower than those from twin-based studies, yet larger than has been accounted for by genome-wide association studies so far.

title: Wanting to matter and learning to care: A neurodevelopmental window of opportunity for (Pro) social learning?
abstract: Wanting to matter-to feel socially recognized, appreciated, and capable of actions that benefit others-represents a fundamental motivation in human development. The motivational salience of mattering appears to increase in adolescence. Evidence suggests this is related to pubertal increases in the incentive salience for gaining social value and personal agency. This can provide a useful heuristic for understanding motivational proclivities (i.e. wanting to matter) that influence action-outcome learning as young adolescents are exploring and learning how to navigate increasingly complex social and relational environments. Adolescence also brings new capacities, motives, and opportunities for learning to care about and contribute to the benefit of others. Together, these create a window of opportunity: a sensitive period for learning to gain salient feelings of mattering through caring prosocial actions and valued societal contributions. Successfully discovering ways of mattering by doing things that matter to others may contribute to formative socio-emotional learning about self/other. Advances in understanding these social and relational learning processes and their neurodevelopmental underpinnings can inform strategies to improve developmental trajectories of social competence and wellbeing among adolescents growing up in a rapidly changing and increasingly techno-centric world.

title: Bibliometric Applications in Social Science Research: The Social Network Context of Generosity
abstract: Whether or not a person chooses to act philanthropically can seem like a personal decision. Yet, giving is inherently a social act, minimally involving a giver and a receiver. The relational aspects of giving decisions can be studied by investigating social networks. What is known about the role of social networks in charitable giving? To answer this question, this study utilizes bibliometric techniques to review existing literature in a systematic manner. Applying these tools to social science research facilitates integration of knowledge across multiple disciplines and diverse methodological approaches. Across the reviewed research, there are five central themes. First, networks can shape values of efforts to support the public good. Second, networks can informally punish people for acting too self-interestedly. Third, networks can join together or exclude, contributing to social inequality and its reproduction over time. Fourth, networks can maintain group dynamics. Fifth, networks can pattern behaviors into habits, form interdependence, situate what is considered normal, and provide stability in times of crisis. Implications of existing research are drawn toward understanding young adulthood within its networked social contexts of generosity.

title: Oxytocin salvages context-specific hyperaltruistic preference through moral framing
abstract: Abstract An intriguing advancement in recent moral decision-making research suggests that people are more willing to sacrifice monetary gains to spare others from suffering than to spare themselves, yielding a hyperaltruistic tendency. Other studies, however, indicate an opposite egoistic bias in that subjects are less willing to harm themselves for the benefits of others than for their own benefits. These results highlight the delicate inner workings of moral decision and call for a mechanistic account of hyperaltruistic preference. We investigated the boundary conditions of hyperaltruism by presenting subjects with trade-off choices combing monetary gains and painful electric shocks, or, choices combing monetary losses and shocks. We first showed in study 1 that switching the decision context from gains to losses effectively eliminated the hyperaltruistic preference and the decision context effect was associated with the altered relationship between subjects’ instrumental harm (IH) trait attitudes and their relative pain sensitivities. In the pre-registered study 2, we tested whether oxytocin, a neuropeptide linked to parochial altruism, might salvage the context-dependent hyperaltruistic preference. We found that oxytocin increased subjects’ reported levels of framing the task as harming (vs. helping) others, which mediated the correlation between IH and relative pain sensitivities. Thus, the loss decision context and oxytocin nullified and restored the mediation effect of subjective harm framing, respectively. Our results help to elucidate the psychological processes underpinning the contextual specificity of hyperaltruism and carry implications in promoting prosocial interactions in our society.

title: Assessing policy readiness for climate-informed infectious disease early warning systems in Vietnam: a scoping review and stakeholder consultation.
abstract: Climate change is reshaping infectious disease patterns, increasing the need for climate-informed early warning systems (EWSs). However, the extent to which Vietnam's governance frameworks support their development and implementation remains unclear. To assess policies and guidelines governing infectious disease EWSs in Vietnam and identify gaps and opportunities to strengthen system readiness. A policy review using a modified scoping review approach was supplemented by qualitative stakeholder consultations. National regulatory documents issued since 2000 and in effect as of July 2026 were identified through Vietnamese legal databases. Documents were analysed thematically and mapped against the core components of EWSs. Twelve key stakeholders were interviewed to contextualise policy findings and explore implementation challenges. Fifteen policy documents met the inclusion criteria. Vietnam has established strong legal and policy foundations for disease reporting, outbreak investigation, emergency response, and intersectoral coordination. Recent policies increasingly recognise climate change adaptation, environmental risks, digital transformation, and cross-sector collaboration, creating an enabling environment for the development of EWSs. However, these policies primarily provide strategic direction and institutional support rather than operational guidance for implementing EWSs. Key gaps include fragmented governance arrangements for data sharing and integration across meteorological, epidemiological, vector, laboratory, and vulnerability datasets; limited guidance on model validation and adoption; weak mechanisms linking forecasts to authorised anticipatory actions; and constraints related to financing and workforce capacity. Strengthening policies and operational guidance for forecasting, data integration, and forecast-based action will be critical to enhancing preparedness for and responses to climate-sensitive infectious diseases in Vietnam.

title: Anions as catalysts: from organosilanes as pro-nucleophiles to base-embedding electrophiles.
abstract: The catalytic activity of neutral and anionic Lewis base catalysts depends on several factors. One is catalyst turnover, which may explain why neutral Lewis bases, such as tertiary amines and phosphines, are widely employed as catalysts in organic synthesis. In this review, we discuss less common strategies by which fluorides, alkoxides, amide anions and related anionic species can be rendered efficient catalysts, including for stereoselective synthesis. We give historical context and highlight recent examples that exploit organosilanes as pro-nucleophiles for challenging bond formation and enantioselective synthesis. The primary emphasis, however, is placed on the use of organosilanes as pro-bases, specifically referred to herein as base-embedding electrophiles (BEE), as part of an idea we wish to conceptualize, as we believe the concept holds substantial yet underappreciated potential in organic synthesis. We focus on how the BEE reagents disentangle traditional Brønsted acid-base considerations from catalyst turnover in substitutions and additions. Existing examples are discussed with particular attention to their conceptual significance. Drawing on these principles, we and others have leveraged base-embedding electrophiles to develop catalytic and stereoselective reactions toward difficult-to-access organic molecules. By sharing this perspective, we hope that readers will also be able to recognize the opportunities and challenges associated with anionic catalysis enabled by organosilanes.

title: Sustainable biobased packaging via integrated robotics/machine learning workflow for improved postharvest preservation.
abstract: Reliance on petroleum-derived plastic packaging exacerbates environmental burdens and lacks intrinsic antimicrobial protection against food spoilage. While biobased materials offer a sustainable alternative, optimizing their formulations is hindered by vast component libraries, inefficient trial-and-error experimentation, and complex multiproperty requirements. Herein, we develop an integrated workflow combining robotic automation, machine learning predictions, density functional theory, and life cycle assessment to accelerate biobased packaging discovery. Leveraging data augmentation and ensemble modeling, we use a hierarchical neural network to predict ∼1 billion candidate formulations, balancing mechanical properties, optical transparency, and environmental footprint. The resulting biobased packaging demonstrates enhanced hydrostability, effective antimicrobial activity, and high barrier performance, significantly extending the shelf life of cucumbers and avocados. Last, we release a data-sharing platform featuring forward prediction, inverse design, and environmental impact functions to support community use. This integrative framework provides sustainable, antimicrobial packaging materials alternative to conventional plastic films.

title: Segment Anything Model-Guided Dual-Branch Swin Transformer with Cross-Attention Fusion for Knee Osteoarthritis Severity Grading on X-ray Images.
abstract: We investigate a Segment Anything Model (SAM)-guided dual-branch Swin Transformer for knee osteoarthritis severity grading from X-ray images. A threshold-assisted SAM pipeline generates bone-region masks without task-specific SAM fine-tuning. Separate Swin-B branches process the image and mask, and two unidirectional cross-attention modules integrate their features. In the reported five-class evaluation, the model achieves 78.80\% accuracy, a macro-averaged one-vs-rest AUC of 0.9588, and quadratic weighted kappa of 0.8780. The corresponding three-class accuracy is 79.58\%. Expanded comparisons include KOA-specific methods and ablations of mask generation, weight sharing, and fusion configuration. These results support the usefulness of combining image context with mask-derived structural information within the evaluated setting.

title: Multi-Task Deep Learning for Joint Depth-Map Reconstruction and Iso-Point Prediction from Hyperspectral Images of Turbid Phantoms.
abstract: Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) of turbid, tissue-mimicking media entangles the geometry of subsurface inclusions with the optical properties of the surrounding matrix in every spectrum. From HSI cubes of polyurethane phantoms with obliquely drilled inclusions we recover two physically distinct quantities: a dense depth map of the inclusion and the scalar iso-point wavelength, the point of near-invariance at which the depth-dependent modulation of the diffuse reflectance cancels. A single multi-task U-Net is a poor compromise for such complementary targets, the dense and scalar heads reaching their optima at different epochs while global pooling destroys the spectral-position information a wavelength target needs. We therefore decompose the problem into two specialised networks sharing one pipeline: a Bin Latent Transformer (BiLT) cross-attention scanner for the iso-point and a masked, zero-padded U-Net for the depth map. Under a strict cross-phantom split the depth network reaches a mean relative error of 6.07±0.71% (R2=0.934±0.014), against 19.4% for the analytic two-band index of earlier work and about 12.9% for the multi-task baseline. Zero-padding with a masked loss, preserving the inclusion-width information that cropping discards, is the decisive ingredient, and conditioning depth on the iso-point yields no further gain. The iso-point network reaches 5.03±0.93 nm RMSE (R2=0.630±0.085) from the spectra alone. Plausible settings of the iso-point detector change the labels themselves by 2.6 to 3.9 nm root-mean-square, while the retrained network stays between 4.8 and 5.3 nm. Together with oracle and per-patch-detection diagnostics, this identifies the ceiling as a detector-limited label-noise floor rather than a model deficiency. Averaging over a whole inclusion lowers the RMSE to a 3.27 nm plateau, separating an averageable random error from an irreducible regression-to-the-mean bias. For the straight, obliquely drilled bores tested here the depth task is solved to deployable accuracy, and the iso-point network gives a useful per-segment estimate where direct optical determination fails.

title: Normal Early Investigations Do Not Exclude Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis: Highlighting Diagnostic and Treatment Pitfalls.
abstract: Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (BBE) is a rare immune-mediated disorder characterized by ophthalmoplegia, cerebellar ataxia, and impaired consciousness. It is now recognized as a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), sharing common pathogenic mechanisms with Miller Fisher syndrome. However, early diagnosis remains challenging, particularly when initial investigations are normal. We report a 20-year-old previously healthy woman presenting with rapidly progressive ophthalmoplegia, bulbar dysfunction, flaccid quadriparesis, areflexia, and impaired consciousness following a febrile upper respiratory illness. Early cerebrospinal fluid analysis and brain MRI were normal. Anti-GQ1b antibodies were positive, and nerve conduction studies showed isolated proximal conduction abnormalities with absent F-waves. The patient developed respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and was treated with an extended course of plasma exchange, resulting in near-complete recovery. This case highlights a critical diagnostic pitfall: BBE, a variant of GBS, can present with a life-threatening brainstem syndrome despite entirely normal early investigations. We emphasize the value of recognizing the paradoxical combination of areflexia and extensor plantar responses and the use of F-wave studies as an early electrophysiological foothold when standard studies are unrevealing. Furthermore, it demonstrates that even in catastrophic, ventilator-dependent presentations, an extended course of plasma exchange can lead to a favorable outcome, suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy for severe presentations of BBE.

title: Supporting high-quality enrollment decision-making in clinical research: development of a novel informed consent communication framework and curriculum.
abstract: In clinical trials, the process of informed consent is intended to support prospective participants in making enrollment decisions that are well informed and aligned with their values and preferences. Despite the importance of relationship building during the consent process, there is little structured guidance for researchers on how to effectively facilitate informed consent conversations with prospective participants. This project aimed to develop and implement a relationship-based communication framework for clinical researchers, with the ultimate goal of supporting prospective participants in making values-aligned decisions. The ENgaging with Values to Inform research enrollment deciSIONs (ENVISION) study was launched to improve the process of research enrollment decision-making within the context of a multisite cystic fibrosis clinical trial. The ENVISION team sought input from individuals with cystic fibrosis, researchers, institutional review board leaders, and clinical research leaders to understand key issues in consent communication in the context of cystic fibrosis trials. A working group of the ENVISION team incorporated these viewpoints into the development of a consent communication framework, which was guided by consideration of elements of the Ottawa Decision Support Framework and incorporated established communication strategies. The communication framework and an accompanying training curriculum were finalized through iterative review with the working group and the full team. The development process resulted in a four-component, values-oriented communication framework, the RIVER framework: Relationship (forming a connection with the prospective participant), Information (sharing about the study), Values Exploration (eliciting and examining relevant values), and Resolution (confirming a values-aligned decision). Each component includes considerations to support prospective participants in making values-aligned decisions. RIVER is implemented through a training curriculum designed for research coordinators. The training curriculum consists of two 2-hour sessions that include didactic teaching, group discussion, and role-play scenarios, which provide an opportunity to practice real-world clinical research enrollment conversations. The RIVER framework offers a structured approach to communication during clinical research consent conversations that is designed to enhance voluntary, informed decisions. Ongoing evaluation of the framework and training curriculum will inform opportunities for future revisions, adaptations, and broader dissemination.

title: Biological, genomic, and biogeographic characterization of two lytic phages infecting Vibrio natriegens.
abstract: Vibrio natriegens is a marine bacterium known for its exceptionally rapid growth and has recently attracted considerable attention as an alternative host microorganism in the field of biotechnology. Despite this growing interest, phages infecting this species remain poorly characterized. In this study, two lytic phages that infect V. natriegens, vB_Vna_AM1 and vB_Vna_AM2, were isolated and subjected to biological characterization and phylogenetic analysis. Phages vB_Vna_AM1 and vB_Vna_AM2 were isolated from the Sumiyō River mangrove area in Amamigunto National Park, Kagoshima, Japan. Their morphology was determined using transmission electron microscopy. One-step growth curve experiments, host-range evaluation, and viability tests under different temperature, salinity, and pH conditions were performed. Whole-genome sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and homology searches against global ocean virome datasets were conducted. vB_Vna_AM1 and vB_Vna_AM2 exhibited prolate capsids and contractile tails, with latent periods of 40-60 min, and both infected V. natriegens specifically among the tested strains. Their genome sizes and GC contents were 244,321 bp and 41.51% for vB_Vna_AM1, and 327,464 bp and 40.67% for vB_Vna_AM2, respectively. Both phages were assigned to a subcluster of other vibriophages, showing similarities of 92.1-92.2% for vB_Vna_AM1 and 86.8-86.9% for vB_Vna_AM2. Homology searches using global ocean virome datasets revealed that homologous genes were distributed globally at the protein level; however, they were detected as partial genes within otherwise diverse viral genomes. This study provides the initial description and phylogenetic analysis of newly isolated phages infecting V. natriegens. These findings expand the currently limited repertoire of culturable phages of V. natriegens and support the concept that gene modules may be shared among diverse phages within a gene-sharing network, contributing to the understanding of marine viral diversity.

title: Language AI enables endogenous topic discovery and behavioral prediction from trust game perceptions
abstract: The Trust Game (and its many variants) is a widely used experimental paradigm for studying trust and prosocial behavior, yet its interpretation remains debated. We demonstrate endogenous topic discovery and labeling via language AI as a scalable complement to traditional methods, uncovering semantic themes not commonly associated with the game. Using 1,124 subjects’ descriptions of Trust Game interactions from two studies, we show that social concerns emerge as key predictors of prosocial behavior, alongside trust-related language, even when the interaction is framed as a loan repayment. The pipeline converts unstructured responses into predictions of individual decisions: we train a cross-validated XGBoost–Random Forest ensemble that classifies prosocial and selfish behavior from topic features alone well above chance (AUC 0.73). Explicit language categorized as risk, gambling, investment, or game-theoretic themes was less informative in models predicting passing than language categorized as trust, teamwork, or involving moral self-image. These findings both validate and challenge conventional assumptions, highlighting the importance of social and moral language in managerial decision-making.

title: When Scarcity Backfires: Identity–Message Fit and Donation Resilience Under Repeated Appeals
abstract: ABSTRACT Scarcity‐framed donation appeals are common, but their ability to sustain donor engagement over time remains unclear. In this research, we investigate when and for whom scarcity framing helps preserve donation resilience, defined as resistance to decline in charitable support across repeated exposures. Across three studies, we show that scarcity framing slows the decline in charitable responses among individuals whose frugal identity is strong, but only when the appeal can be interpreted as supporting efficient and meaningful use of resources. Study 1 demonstrates that scarcity appeals increase donation resilience among frugal individuals but not among nonfrugal individuals. Study 2 identifies an important boundary condition by showing that this effect emerges for relatively resource‐stable causes but disappears for causes characterized by chronic resource scarcity. Study 3 replicates the identity–message fit effect using actual donation behavior. Together, these results demonstrate that scarcity is not inherently motivating or discouraging; its effects depend on the fit between identity and contextual meaning.

title: Coevolution of norm psychology and cooperation through exapted conformity.
abstract: People willingly follow norms and values, often incurring material costs. This behaviour supposedly stems from evolved norm psychology, contributing to large-scale cooperation among humans. It has been argued that cooperation is influenced by two types of norms: injunctive and descriptive. This study theoretically explores the socialisation of humans under these norms. Our agent-based model simulates scenarios where diverse agents with heterogeneous norm psychologies engage in collective action to maximise their utility functions that capture three motives: gaining material payoff, following injunctive and descriptive norms. Multilevel selective pressure drives the evolution of norm psychology that affects the utility function. Further, we develop a model with exapted conformity, assuming selective advantage for descriptive norm psychology. We show that norm psychology can evolve via cultural group selection. We then identify two normative conditions that favour the evolution of norm psychology, and therefore cooperation: injunctive norms promoting punitive behaviour and descriptive norms. Furthermore, we delineate different characteristics of cooperative societies under these two conditions and explore the potential for a macro transition between them. Together, our results validate the emergence of large-scale cooperative societies through social norms and suggest complementary roles that conformity and punishment play in human prosociality.

title: Cognitive Mechanism of Influence of Subjective Social Class on Prosocial Risky Behaviour
abstract: ABSTRACT Prosocial risky behaviour (PRB) combines risk and prosociality, defined as risk‐taking for the benefit of others or society. Its differences across subjective social classes and underlying mechanisms are unclear. Study 1 ( n = 590) used a questionnaire to explore the relationship between subjective social class and PRB. Study 2 ( n = 120) manipulated subjective social class and set risk levels in prosocial risky dilemmas to examine causal relationships and boundary conditions. Study 3 ( n = 120) used cognitive computational modelling to clarify effects and explore cognitive mechanisms. Results showed the following: (1) subjective social class negatively predicts PRB, especially in the 30%–50% risk range; (2) low social class individuals have lower loss aversion, higher guilt aversion and value PRB more; (3) two decision preferences parallel mediate the relationship between subjective social class and PRB. These findings offer insights for mitigating social class differences’ negative impacts and enhancing prosocial levels in risky situations.

title: Mechanisms and Outcomes of User-Led Online Peer-to-Peer Support for Individuals With Schizophrenia: A Netnographic Study in Japan.
abstract: Social networking services are increasingly used by individuals with mental illnesses to share experiences and provide mutual support. However, information about how people with schizophrenia engage in these online spaces and how their participation contributes to recovery is scarce. This study aimed to elucidate the mechanisms and outcomes of user-led online peer-to-peer support for individuals with schizophrenia within a LINE-based online community in Japan. A qualitative netnographic approach, guided by the LiLEDDA method, was employed. This study involved a secondary analysis of a previously collected blog corpus. Of 916 posts published between January 2018 and February 2025, 143 entries were selected for analysis. Data were analysed inductively using thematic analysis. Three interrelated themes were identified: (1) Affordances for Participation, (2) Mechanisms of Support and (3) Perceived Recovery-Related Outcomes. Participation was facilitated by self-regulated engagement, loose ties and light governance: balancing freedom and safety. These affordances enabled mechanisms of hope and self-redefinition through role modelling, empathy-informed practical advice, and the provision of an empathic safe space. Participants described these mechanisms as contributing to perceived recovery-related outcomes, including reduced anxiety and distress, social withdrawal and increased motivation. Online safety and trust also supported the development of offline connections, creating a hybrid, self-reinforcing recovery cycle. These findings suggest a hybrid recovery model linking digital and physical connectedness. Trust and empathy cultivated online translated into offline belonging, while offline experiences reinforced online engagement. Participants described low-intensity, multimodal communication as helping to reduce social withdrawal and support graded reintegration into social life. The mechanisms were further shaped by Japan's collectivist, high-context culture, where harmony and 'loose ties' sustained participation. Thus, user-led online peer communities may represent culturally attuned, recovery-oriented environments that complement traditional mental healthcare.

title: A Multistage Fine-Tuning and Empathy Alignment Approach for an Emotional Support Dialogue System: Development and Evaluation Study.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for text-based emotional support. However, general-purpose LLMs may not consistently recognize emotional cues, adapt supportive strategies to contexts, or generate responses aligned with psychologically informed communication. The limited availability of large-scale, structured Chinese counseling data further constrains the development of models for context-sensitive emotional support. We developed and evaluated YuanChat, a family of specialized LLMs for context-sensitive emotional support; assessed whether E-URIAL improved response quality; and compared YuanChat with base LLMs. We constructed 2 datasets from anonymized real-world counseling sessions: ECD-3 (104,897 counselor response turns) for fine-tuning and Fine-tuning increased YuanChat-Huozi3.5's empathic expression score from 0.57 to 0.68; empathy identification score increased from 0.54 to 0.59. In expert evaluation, YuanChat-Huozi3.5 received a higher empathic attunement score than the base Huozi3.5 model (1.279 vs 0.327; mean difference 0.952, 95% CI 0.746-1.152). Using professional counselor responses as the reference, the mean differences for YuanChat-Huozi3.5 were 0.148, 0.079, 0.039, and 0.002 in empathic attunement, supportive appropriateness, perceived helpfulness, and safety and professional boundary adherence, respectively. No statistically significant differences were detected between YuanChat-Huozi3.5 and the counselor references (all Holm-adjusted The findings indicate that fine-tuning on real-world counseling data and annotating models with structured emotional support labels improved context-sensitive empathic responding in LLMs. Without updating model parameters, E-URIAL further improved empathy identification and empathic expression across multiple models. Together, these methods provide a scalable, theory-informed approach to enhancing the emotional support capabilities of LLMs.

title: Tibiotalocalcaneal Fusion Using Hindfoot Nailing Versus Open Reduction and Internal Fixation for Fragility Ankle Fractures in Older Adults: A Prospective Randomized Comparative Study.
abstract: Fragility ankle fractures in older adults are challenging because poor bone quality, medical comorbidities, and vulnerable soft tissues increase the risk of fixation failure, wound complications, and prolonged immobilization after conventional open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF). Tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) fusion using a hindfoot intramedullary nail may provide stable load-sharing fixation while allowing earlier weight bearing. TTC fusion using a hindfoot nail would provide better 12-month functional outcomes, earlier weight bearing and radiological union, and fewer fixation-related complications than ORIF in older adults with fragility ankle fractures. This prospective, single-center, parallel-group randomized controlled study included 60 patients aged ≥65 years with fragility ankle fractures, with 30 patients treated by TTC fusion and 30 by ORIF. Each participant was followed for 12 months. The primary outcome was the Olerud-Molander Ankle Score (OMAS) at 12 months. Secondary outcomes included the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) Ankle-Hindfoot Score, time to weight bearing, radiological union and time to union, midfoot range of motion, and postoperative complications. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06709365). The TTC group had a significantly shorter operative time than the ORIF group (62.4 ± 9.8 vs. 89.7 ± 12.3 min; p < 0.001) and achieved earlier weight bearing (2.1 ± 1.3 vs. 9.2 ± 2.4 weeks; p < 0.001). At 12 months, OMAS was significantly higher in the TTC group (75.77 ± 4.02 vs. 65.57 ± 4.54; p < 0.001), as was the AOFAS score (80.17 ± 4.95 vs. 69.00 ± 4.94; p < 0.001). Radiological union occurred in 28/30 patients (93.3%) after TTC fusion and 26/30 (86.7%) after ORIF (p = 0.67), while time to union was significantly shorter after TTC fusion (12.1 ± 2.3 vs. 14.6 ± 3.1 weeks; p = 0.0008). Postoperative midfoot range of motion was also greater in the TTC group (36.8 ± 6.4 ° vs. 31.4 ± 5.8 °; p = 0.001). TTC fusion with a hindfoot nail provided superior 12-month functional outcomes, earlier weight bearing, shorter operative time, and faster radiological union than ORIF in selected older adults with fragility ankle fractures. However, the observed reduction in individual complications was not statistically significant, and the permanent loss of ankle and subtalar motion together with the limited 12-month follow-up should be considered when selecting treatment. title: The Largesse design problem
abstract: Abstract Largesse design is a positive theory of what happens when players in a game, who have a limited willingness to sacrifice for the common good, can coordinate on a welfare-optimal solution. This theory provides an alternative to psychological theories in explaining why players engage in costly punishments and rewards. It also says that players will engage in other low-cost methods of encouraging pro-social behavior, for example, through reputation effects. In this paper, I study the properties and comparative statics of the largesse design problem. Despite a lack of concavity in the maximization problem, solutions are unique and continuous except on a lower-dimensional bifurcation set. In examples, I study these bifurcations, in which a small change in the parameters can lead to a large change in behavior or welfare.

title: Adolescent Prosocial and Antisocial Behaviours: Simultaneous Effects of Self-control, Attitudes of Parents and Teachers
abstract: This study investigates the complex relationships between parental attitudes, teacher attitudes, and self-control and their associations with prosocial and antisocial behaviour among adolescents in Bali, Indonesia. The research utilises a correlational research design with structural equation modelling (SEM) analysis to examine the relationships among variables comprehensively. A sample of 260 high school students aged 14 to 16 in Bali, Indonesia, was selected using a multi-stage cluster random sampling technique with 104 male and 156 female. The standard deviation of age is 0.49. Data were collected using adapted instruments to measure prosocial behaviour, antisocial behaviour, parents’ attitudes, teachers’ attitudes, and self-control. The study found positive correlations between parental attitudes, teacher attitudes, self-control, and prosocial behaviour and negative correlations with antisocial behaviour. The SEM analysis produced a predictive model for adolescent prosocial and antisocial behaviour, demonstrating strong compatibility with the model. The results indicated that parents’ attitudes, teachers’ attitudes, and self-control contributed significantly to prosocial behaviour among adolescents. However, while teachers’ attitudes and self-control were significantly related to antisocial behaviour, no significant relationship was found between parents’ attitudes and antisocial behaviour. The findings provide valuable insights into the role of parent-child relationships and highlight the potential for fostering positive behavioural outcomes. The study’s contribution lies in its focus on multiple dimensions of relationships and its exploration of the impact of parental difficulties. Ultimately, this research deepens the understanding of prosocial and antisocial behaviour and its underlying mechanisms, shedding new light on the field of prosocial.

title: The Moderating role of Empathy in the Relationship Between Extraversion and Online Prosocial Behaviour
abstract: Online prosocial behaviour (OPB) encompasses actions performed in online environments such as social media platforms, that are intended to benefit others. OPB may be associated with extraversion, as it may involve engagement in social environments and understanding others' emotions and thoughts, particularly when they require assistance. The impact of varying levels of empathy on socioemotional outcomes remain debated. The aim of the current study was to investigate the moderating role of empathy in the relationship between OPB and extraversion. A total of 248 university students (Mage=20.75, SD=1.56; range =18-25, Nfemale=170, 68.5%) participated in the study. The moderating role of empathy was examined. The research results demonstrated a positive correlation between OPB and extraversion among individuals with low and moderate levels of empathy. However, this correlation was not observed among young adults with high levels of empathy. The results have shown that extraversion does not predict OPB in individuals with high empathy, whereas extraversion is significantly associated with OPB among those with low and moderate levels of empathy.

title: The Moderating Role of Nepotism Perception in The Relationship Between Prosocial Behavior and Superego
abstract: This study examines the relationship between superego and prosocial behavior and the moderating role of the perception of nepotism in this relationship. A total of 260 employees from various sectors participated in the study. Using the self-reporting method, participants evaluated their perception of superego, prosocial behavior, and nepotism. According to the findings, a positive relationship was found between the superego levels of the employees and their prosocial behavior levels. At the same time, a negative relationship was found between the prosocial behavior levels of the employees and their perception of nepotism. It also did not play a moderating role in the relationship between nepotism, superego, and prosocial behavior. The findings are discussed in detail in the discussion section, and suggestions for future research are presented. In conclusion, although this study conducted on a limited sample, it contributes to the examination of the test of psychological and social psychological assumptions in an organizational context.

title: Using Theory of Change Models to Evaluate the Implementation of Urinary Incontinence Management in Primary Care Initiatives.
abstract: Theory of change (ToC) models articulate how and why implementation interventions are expected to produce specific outcomes and can guide both program design and evaluation. As part of a theory-driven evaluation for a federal initiative to improve non-surgical management of urinary incontinence among women in primary care, we co-developed ToC models for five funded projects. Each model depicted intervention approaches, hypothesized mechanisms of change, and expected outcomes. Using a six-step process which included document review, consensus-based element identification, open coding, iterative refinement, and stakeholder validation, we created and refined a separate ToC for each grantee. The Technical Expert Panel, convened for the broader initiative, provided multidisciplinary feedback to ensure methodological rigor and contextual accuracy. Sharing the models in annual meetings supported cross-grantee learning and revealed common implementation themes: reliance on technology-based patient education and clinician training, challenges with practice recruitment, tailored facilitation to reduce clinician burden, and gaps in patient-level evaluation measures. The ToC models served four primary functions: orientation for evaluators, technical assistance for grantees, monitoring and evaluation of implementation processes, and cross-site collaboration. Key lessons included the importance of early stakeholder engagement, flexibility in model development, and the value of visual tools for communication and shared understanding. Although resource requirements and retrospective development were challenges, ToC models proved to be adaptable, dynamic tools that enhance evaluation and collaboration in complex, multi-site health initiatives. Their systematic application can strengthen future national and international implementation efforts.

title: The Role of Family Climate in Shaping the Moral Development of University Students: A Systematic Review
abstract: This review methodically explores the role of family climate in the formation and learning of moral values among university students.Being the key agent of socialization, the family is central to the development of the moral structure of young adults in their early life and in the process of transitioning to higher education.This review is based on empirical studies conducted mainly in the Indian context, with some international comparisons, to determine the key dimensions of family climate that impact moral development.The thematic areas under investigation are parenting styles and their various effects on moral reasoning; how emotional attachment and family cohesion contribute to the development of prosocial behavior; cultural and religious factors in value formation; the effects of family structure and socioeconomic status on moral orientation; and how technology and digital media are increasingly shaping contemporary moral socialization.The results indicate that authoritative parenting, which is typified by warmth, open communication, and discipline based on reasoning, is most strongly related to greater levels of moral competence among university students.Affective attachment in families plays a pivotal role in mediating family based value transfers, and collectivist cultural standards in the Indian context uphold family based moral education.The review also notes considerable gaps in the research, such as the lack of longitudinal studies investigating the trajectories of moral development, underresearched demographic factors such as caste and regional diversity, and under-researched moderating factors such as peer groups and institutional environments.The results can be of great significance to institutions of learning that want to incorporate value education into their curriculum and to policymakers who want to develop family supportive systems that integrate the comprehensive development of students.

title: The nanotubular network as a new dimension of intercellular communication in the nervous system.
abstract: Communication between cells in the nervous system has long been understood to occur through chemical and electrical synapses, and through the release of signalling molecules and extracellular vesicles across the extracellular space. Intercellular nanotubes (NTs) - thin, membranous tubular bridges that physically connect distant cells - represent a structurally distinct route of communication, enabling the direct, targeted transfer of cellular cargoes between selected cells. Once studied almost exclusively in culture, NTs have now been visualized in situ and in vivo throughout the nervous system, including dendritic NTs between neurons, NTs formed by microglia and astrocytes, interpericyte NTs in the retina and NTs between satellite glia and peripheral sensory neurons. Through these connections, cells exchange mitochondria, proteins and their aggregates, and calcium, supporting three emerging roles: homeostatic rescue of stressed cells, pathological propagation of toxic proteins in neurodegeneration and non-synaptic calcium signalling, respectively. NT networks are dynamic and stress-responsive, suggesting that they provide a plastic infrastructure for resource sharing among neurons and glia. Understanding their function will require establishing a standardized definition, achieving rigorous in situ validation and quantification, and developing specific molecular tools to manipulate NTs.

title: When the brain says "No!": An MRI study on the neural correlates of resistance to immoral orders.
abstract: Milgram's studies explored psychological and contextual factors influencing (dis)obedience to immoral orders, but the mechanisms preventing individuals from being coerced into causing pain to others remained largely unknown. Our fMRI study investigated the neural correlates of disobedience to such orders, focusing on three phases of the decision-making process: order processing (predecision), action (decision), and outcome and effect processing (postdecision). Within these phases we targeted three sociocognitive (cognitive conflict, sense of agency-SoA, and theory of mind-ToM) and two socioaffective (empathy and guilt) processes. Our findings revealed that participants who engaged the angular gyrus and temporoparietal junction, particularly in the left hemisphere, as well as median prefrontal areas before obeying the command to send a shock-possibly to mitigate cognitive conflict between self and other and to enhance their SoA-were more likely to disobey the experimenter's instructions to administer a shock to a victim. Additionally, we found involvement of social brain regions during the postdecision phase (encompassing ToM, empathy, and guilt areas), especially in response to shock events, to process the victim's pain. Higher activity in these regions when obeying orders was associated with a higher rate of prosocial disobedience. This study sheds light on the mechanisms that lead individuals to resist immoral actions under authoritative pressure in an experimental context.

title: A Review of the Philosophical Foundations of Islamic Rules and Ethics in Zurkhaneh Sports Architecture
abstract: Zurkhaneh, the traditional Iranian “house of strength,” represents more than a setting for physical exercise. Its ritual practices integrate bodily training, heroic narratives, music, religious symbolism, hierarchical etiquette, and ethical instruction. This review examines the philosophical and cultural foundations through which Islamic moral values, the tradition of futuwwa or javanmardi (chivalry), Shi’i symbolism, Sufi ethical concepts, and older Iranian traditions have been interpreted within Zurkhaneh sport and architecture. The study adopts a qualitative library-review approach and critically synthesizes historical scholarship, peer-reviewed research, reference works, and cultural-heritage documentation concerning Pahlavani and Zurkhaneh traditions. Particular attention is given to the relationship between ethical instruction and architectural form, including the sunken gowd, the sardam of the morshed, ritual hierarchy, symbolic sporting instruments, poetry, music, and collective practice. The review indicates that Zurkhaneh culture historically linked strength with humility, self-restraint, generosity, loyalty, respect for elders, protection of the vulnerable, and service to the community. These values are closely related to the ethical vocabulary of futuwwa/javanmardi and, in later Iranian contexts, to Shi’i devotion and the exemplary status attributed to Imam Ali. At the same time, the historical origins of the institution remain contested; similarities with older Iranian and Mithraic traditions should therefore be treated as interpretive hypotheses rather than as evidence of an uninterrupted institutional genealogy. Contemporary scholarship likewise shows that Zurkhaneh has evolved substantially over time. The continuing significance of the institution lies not in reproducing a fixed historical form, but in understanding how architecture, ritual, physical training, collective memory, and moral education can operate together. This integrated model provides a useful basis for discussing ethical formation in sport while avoiding romanticized contrasts between traditional and modern athletic practice.

title: Individual and group characteristics and their economic implications
abstract: This thesis is a collection of studies about the link between individual and group characteristics and economic outcomes. The firstt chapter investigates the link between declared trusting attitudes and trust choices in an infinitely repeated trust game after controlling for subjective beliefs. It is found that intrinsic trust influences the probability of trusting in a trust game. Moreover, intrinsic trust seems to operate through the fact that more trusting individuals are more likely to forgive or offer the bene t of doubt to others and show trust even after a disappointing outcome. The effect of intrinsic trust appears to be independent of the formation of beliefs. The second chapter studies personality trait variation and its implications on society's welfare. Personality is taken to be a type of skill that can be better understood if considered as a distribution rather than a single point. The ABM simulation results reported show that population personality compositions are adaptive on the task (job) distribution. Further simulation results depict the importance for appropriate education to cater for the jobs in the economy. Finally, simulations indicate that precise job match screening is beneficial not only for society's welfare but also for subjective well-being. The third chapter is concerned with how intelligence affects the social outcomes of groups. A systematic study of the link is provided in an experiment where two groups of subjects with different levels of intelligence, but otherwise similar, play a repeated prisoner's dilemma. Initial cooperation rates are similar, but increase in the groups with higher intelligence to reach almost full cooperation, while they decline in the groups with lower intelligence. Cooperation of higher intelligence subjects is payoff sensitive and not automatic: in a treatment with lower continuation probability there is no difference between different intelligence groups

title: Social Sharing of Emotion and Wellbeing at Work: Current Practices and the Emerging Role of Conversational Agents
abstract: Employee well-being has become an urgent organizational priority in response to rising rates of occupational stress, burnout, and mental health challenges across industries. Traditional well-being initiatives—such as employee assistance programs and wellness interventions—are often hindered by low engagement, social stigma, and limited relevance to workplace-specific stressors. Digital strategies, particularly conversational agents (CAs), present a promising avenue for scalable and personalized support. While CAs have demonstrated potential in healthcare contexts, their role in organizational well-being remains underexplored. This dissertation examines the potential of CAs as tools to support workplace well-being by focusing on the social sharing of emotion among emergency department (ED) clinicians. Using semi-structured interviews, the study investigated how clinicians share emotions at work, what motivates or hinders such practices, and how they perceive institutional support. Findings reveal that clinicians engage in both informal and formal social sharing, with motivations grounded in relational trust, professional identity, and coping needs, but also encounter barriers such as hierarchical constraints, cultural norms, and time pressures. Building on these insights, the study explored opportunities and concerns surrounding the use of CAs for workplace social sharing of emotion and emotional support. While participants recognized potential benefits of implementing the technology such as accessibility, anonymity, and contextual flexibility, concerns were raised regarding trust, privacy, and organizational fit. The dissertation contributes to academic literature and organizational practice by emphasizing the importance of contextual and cultural adaptability, along with trust-building strategies, in designing CAs that fit organizational settings. Ultimately, the study enhances understanding of how social sharing of emotion occurs and how CAs can support efforts to promote wellbeing, providing implications for both CA design and broader organizational support systems.

title: Adolescents During the Pandemic: Supportive and In-Person Rather Than Digital Social Connections Are Associated With Lower Sadness.
abstract: Social connections support emotional well-being and act as buffer against depression during challenging life episodes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, adolescent's social connectedness was disrupted. Here, we examined the association between social connectedness and sadness in a large US sample of adolescents during the pandemic. As part of the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development Study, adolescents completed two online surveys around May (n = 5,298, mage: 12.5 years, 49.7% female) and August 2020 (n = 5,051, mage: 12.7, 49.0% female), including the National Institute of Health Toolbox Sadness Questionnaire short form, and questions about relationship quality, parent-child engagement, and digital connections. Mixed linear models tested associations between social connection and sadness with time points as covariate, sadness was compared between clusters sharing social characteristics. In independent models, household conflicts were associated with higher sadness (p < .01), whereas positive parent-child engagement and relationships, such as having dinner together and talking with parents about plans, were associated with lower sadness (p < .01). Texting, social media, and video chat time were associated with greater sadness (p < .01). Clusters with lower digital communications, stronger parent-child engagement, and better relationships, showed the lowest sadness score. Shifting to less digital connections from May to August was associated with a stronger sadness decrease (p < .01). In-person, rather than digital, and nonconflictual social connections were associated with lower sadness in adolescents in the pandemic context, emphasizing differences between proximal and remote social connections, and possible emotional costs of over-reliance on remote, digital forms of interaction.

title: The Neural Mechanism Underlying Differentiated In-Group Versus Out-Group Face Recognition and Memory, Identification, Empathy and Pro-social Behavior: Evidence from fMRI and ERP Studies
abstract: In the context of perceiving individuals within and outside of social groups, there are distinct cognitive processes and mechanisms in the brain. Extensive research in recent years has delved into the neural mechanisms that underlie differences in how we perceive individuals from different social groups. To gain a deeper understanding of these neural mechanisms, we present a comprehensive review from the perspectives of facial recognition and memory, intergroup identification, empathy, and pro-social behavior. Specifically, we focus on studies that utilize functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and event-related potential (ERP) techniques to explore the relationship between brain regions and behavior. Findings from fMRI studies reveal that the brain regions associated with intergroup differentiation in perception and behavior do not operate independently but instead exhibit dynamic interactions. Similarly, ERP studies indicate that the amplitude of neural responses shows various combinations in relation to perception and behavior.
