title: Family-Inclusive Interventions Supporting Complementary Feeding for Children Aged 6-23 Months: A Scoping Review of Alignment with Family-Centered Care Principles.
abstract: Suboptimal complementary-feeding practices remain an important concern for child nutrition and growth. WHO and UNICEF guidance emphasizes appropriate complementary feeding for children aged 6-23 months, including dietary adequacy, responsive feeding, and supportive caregiving. Because many interventions primarily target mothers, broader family involvement may be underrepresented. This scoping review aimed to map the characteristics, implementation strategies, and reported outcomes of family-inclusive complementary-feeding interventions and examined their alignment with established Family-Centered Care (FCC) principles. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and PRISMA-ScR recommendations. PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL via EBSCOhost, and ScienceDirect were searched for English- or Indonesian-language primary intervention or programme-evaluation studies with extractable quantitative data published from January 2016 to May 3, 2026. Eligibility was structured using the Population, Concept, and Context framework, and included publications were synthesized descriptively and mapped against established FCC principles. Eleven publications representing 10 underlying studies or trials met the eligibility criteria. Information Sharing and Participation were evident in all 11 publications, Dignity and Respect in eight, and explicit Collaboration in two. Across the 10 underlying studies or trials, four recurring family-inclusive patterns were identified: paternal engagement, family empowerment and teamwork, responsive parenting, and community ecosystem integration. These were interpreted as evidence-informed descriptive categories rather than validated FCC dimensions. Reported outcomes were heterogeneous, with favorable findings for selected feeding, caregiver, parenting, growth, and developmental outcomes alongside null or mixed findings. Family-inclusive interventions commonly incorporated information sharing and active caregiver participation, whereas explicit partnership-oriented Collaboration was less frequently reported. Future research should examine how FCC principles can be intentionally operationalized and evaluated in relation to implementation, sustainability, and contextual adaptation. This conceptual mapping may inform future intervention development without implying comparative effectiveness.

title: What Strategies Are Used to Market Digital Gambling to Young People?: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Research indicates that digital gambling, including through online sites and smartphone apps, is an increasing issue among youth. The aim of this scoping review is to identify and map literature exploring how digital strategies are used to market digital gambling products to young people. This scoping review used the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology, with results mapped to the VicHealth Harmful Industries Digital Marketing to Australian Children framework. The review was guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist. Medline (via PubMed), Embase (via Elsevier), Web of Science (via Clarivate), CINAHL (via EbscoHOST), and APA PsycInfo (via EbscoHOST) databases were searched from 2008 to 2025. Title and abstract screening were conducted on 6,069 studies, resulting in 304 articles for full-text screening. After full-text screening, 56 articles met the inclusion criteria for this scoping review. Several included studies described social media marketing as being the prevalent form of promotion of digital gambling products, including sharing of posts and "influencer" promotion of gambling products, with a tendency to normalize gambling behavior among youth. Chance-based mechanisms present in gaming, including loot boxes and simulated gambling, were also described as strong determinants of future problematic gambling. Understanding emerging strategies that gambling companies use to advertise, market, and promote gambling products is essential to provide effective nursing assessment and treatment to young people impacted by problem online gambling.

title: How Artistic Expression Fosters Compassion in Future Engineers: From Sympathy to Empathy to Compassion
abstract: Background: Engineering education has long prioritized technical mastery while marginalizing emotional awareness, ethical reflection, and social responsibility. This technocratic and meritocratic culture often limits engineers’ capacity to address human dimensions of sociotechnical problems. Emerging frameworks such as compassion in engineering propose integrating emotional intelligence, moral imagination, and social concern into professional formation. Purpose/Hypothesis: This study examines how engineering students express compassion through an interdisciplinary course integrating the arts and engineering. We analyze how students conveyed compassion in written and artistic work and how they linked it to engineering practice. Design/Method: Using qualitative thematic analysis, we examined artifacts from an eight-week undergraduate course titled Compassionate Engineering. Results: Students’ ethical awareness was interpreted through a cognitive–affective empathy heuristic. Artistic expression served as medium and method, enabling students to externalize emotion, critique systemic harms, and communicate ethical insights to public audiences. The process reframed design’s Define–Develop phase as a space for ethical imagination and revealed tensions between compassion and competition in engineering culture. Conclusions: Integrating arts-based pedagogies can foster compassionate engineers who approach design as an ethical, creative, and socially responsive practice. Such integration broadens engineering education beyond technical competence toward care, justice, and human-centered responsibility.

title: How large language models judge and influence human cooperation
abstract: Abstract Humans increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to support decisions in social settings. Previous work suggests that such tools can shape people’s moral judgments. However, how LLMs evaluate decisions in social dilemmas, and the long-term implications of LLM-based assessments on human cooperation—driven by indirect reciprocity, reputations, and the capacity to judge interactions of others—remain unclear. We evaluate the social norms of 21 state-of-the-art LLMs when judging more than 40,000 fictitious decisions in social dilemmas. Through an evolutionary game-theoretical model, we study prosociality in populations adhering to these norms, theoretically studying their potential impact on long-term human cooperation. We observe a remarkable agreement in LLMs when evaluating actions against opponents perceived as good. Yet, there is large within- and between-model variance when assessing actions toward ill-reputed individuals. Our theoretical analysis reveals that these differences can significantly impact the prevalence of cooperation within our model. Finally, we show that prompt-based interventions can steer LLM norms, particularly when these define objective goals. Our theoretical model links LLM-based advice to long-term social dynamics, highlighting the importance of designing LLM norms considering their potential effects on human cooperation.

title: The paradox of effective altruism
abstract: Abstract Normative reasoning within the mainstream economic framework has been largely shaped by utilitarian ethics. The growing popularity of effective altruism indicates that the utilitarian spirit has also permeated the sphere of social sentiment, evaluating our pro-social behaviour and charitable giving in terms of efficiency. The present study assesses the appropriateness of judging social outcomes through the prism of allocative efficiency by questioning to what extent the society of effective altruists is robust, sustainable, and resilient. Using computer simulations based on the dictator game, we demonstrate that a society of welfare-maximising effective altruists can achieve an optimal outcome alongside equality under extremely restrictive assumptions, such as the uniformity of giving strategies (i.e. interacting with other effective altruists exclusively) and initial equality of wealth distribution. Yet, in the world of unequal opportunities, utilitarian giving tends to increase wealth disparity. In addition, in polymorphic societies, effective altruists underperform compared to deontological (or unconditional) altruists. Consequently, we demonstrate that striving for allocative efficiency might undermine the equality and resilience objectives and question whether the former should remain the dominant economic normative principle.

title: Video Games and Players’ Empathy, Compassion, and Sympathy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Due to the importance of empathy, the popularity of video games, and the potential contributions to the Differential Susceptibility to Media Effects Model (DSMM), this thesis examined the relationship between video games and empathy-related constructs, including compassion and sympathy. Based on 84 previous studies, this systematic review revealed associations between video games and empathy-related constructs, as well as the diversity in the empathy-related concepts measured by scholars and the instruments used to measure these concepts. A meta-analysis based on 18 studies supported the superior positive impact of prosocial gaming content on players' state empathy, compared to violent video games, neutral video games, and other formats of education such as reading textbooks. This synthesis and integration of research findings support both existing and new propositions for the DSMM

title: Consensus statement from the International Society of Glomerular Disease for Certification of Centers of Excellence in Glomerular Disease.
abstract: In 2022, the International Society of Glomerular Disease (ISGD) was created to be a professional hub for the worldwide community of physicians, researchers, and other stakeholders interested in understanding, treating, and improving the outcomes of glomerular diseases (GDs). The Peer Support Committee of the ISGD seeks to provide support for ISGD members and the broader nephrology community to improve the care of patients with GD, assisting in diagnosis, treatment, and education. To achieve these goals, ISGD seeks to identify and certify Centers of Excellence (COEs) to provide comprehensive care for patients with GD, train the next generation of GD experts, conduct impactful GD research, and advocate for GD as a field of study and practice. In addition, COEs will facilitate mentorship and resource sharing to aid in the formation and development of additional COEs. In this white paper, we present the Consensus Statement of the ISGD for Certification of COEs in GD. Criteria outlined will help ensure that this consensus statement fulfills the 4 mission areas of the program: clinical expertise, research, education, and advocacy. The criteria have been developed to be aspirational and rigorous, yet inclusive. In 2025, ISGD joined forces with GlomCon to create a unified COE program, leveraging each organization's strengths. Short-term goals include disseminating and implementing the standards for certification of COEs in GD, as well as releasing an application in 2026. Longer-term goals include data collection and analysis, increased collaboration among centers, resource sharing, mentorship between centers, and the establishment of clinical trial networks and patient support groups.

title: Long-term music instruction is partially associated with the development of socioemotional skills.
abstract: This study aims to investigate the development of pitch-matching, rhythmic entrainment, and socioemotional skills in children who received formal music instruction and other non-music based after school programs. Eighty-three children, averaging 6.81 years old at baseline, were enrolled in either a music, sports, or no after-school program and followed over four years. The music program involved formal and systematic instruction in music theory, instrumental technique, and performance. Most control participants had no music education; however, in some instances, participants received minimal music education at school or at church. Musical development was measured using a pitch-matching and drumming-based rhythmic entrainment task. Sharing behavior was measured using a variation of the dictator game, and empathy was assessed using three different assessments: the Index of Empathy for Children and Adolescence (trait empathy), the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (theory of mind), and a Fiction Emotion-Matching task (state empathy). Results revealed no time-related associations in pitch-matching ability; however, formal music instruction improved pitch-matching relative to controls. On the contrary, improvements in rhythmic entrainment were best explained by age-related changes rather than music instruction. This study also found limited support for a positive association between formal music instruction and socioemotional skills. That is, individuals with formal music instruction exhibited improved emotion-matching relative to those with sports training. In terms of general socioemotional development, children's trait-level affective empathy did not improve over time, while sharing, theory of mind, and state empathy did. Additionally, pitch-matching and rhythmic entrainment did not reliably predict any socioemotional measures, with associations being trivial to small. While formal music instruction benefitted pitch-matching ability and emotion-matching to an audiovisual stimulus, it was not a significant predictor of rhythmic entrainment or broader socioemotional development. These findings suggest that the transfer of music training may be most evident in near or similar domains.

title: Relational Staging of Digital Atmosphere: Kama Muta, Breakpoints, Ethical Design Guidelines
abstract: This thesis investigates how atmospheric aesthetics in digital art exhibitions shape kama muta, understood as being moved by intensified communal sharing. Focusing on projection-mapped environments, it argues that immersive emotion is not produced by technological spectacle alone but emerges through relational staging, where multisensory design, spatial sequencing, visitor pacing and co-presence condition how audiences interpret and inhabit the exhibition over time. Using Van Gogh: The Immersive Experience (London) as a single commercial case, the study employs an interview-centred qualitative design analysed through Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, supported by six rounds of participant observation and a reflexive autoethnographic log. Twentyfive adults were interviewed (semi-structured and in-depth), sampled for variation in nationality, art background, visit history and viewing mode. Findings are synthesised into a chained thematic model of five themes. Atmospheric envelopment and sensory congruence create temporal holding that prepares receptivity. Co-presence operates through quiet intimacy and gentle witnessing, helping visitors attune to and join a shared tempo without instruction. Traces, low-threshold co-creation and exit continuity form afterglow infrastructure that extends meaning through remembering and sharing. The chain is disrupted by breakpoints, where commercial insertions, visible technology or circulation problems puncture continuity and recast visitors as customers, evaluators or problem-solvers. Threshold moderators (expectations, perceived value, accessibility and visitor background) shape whether relational cues are taken up as credible evidence of communal sharing. The thesis advances a relational staging account of projection-mapped atmosphere and affect, reframes breakpoints and thresholds as structural limits of emotional design under commercial conditions, and translates the mechanism into practical ethical design guidelines prioritising temporal holding, joinability, afterglow protection and transparent threshold governance, with visitor agency, informed choice and psychological safety as baseline requirements.

title: Ternary Moral Empathy Model from the Perspective of Intersubjective Phenomenology.
abstract: The phenomenon of empathy is an intersubjective process of feeling and a particular form of intentionality. Moral empathy refers to a type of empathy that can trigger moral action, with the embodied intersubjectivity laying the foundation for its emergence. This paper attempts to propose a comprehensive theoretical model of moral empathy from the perspective of intersubjective phenomenology, which includes the following. (1) The moral dimension of perceptual empathy: at the subpersonal, unconscious, and perceptual-motor level, embodied empathic practices are essential for the formation of moral consciousness and the emergence of moral empathy. (2) The moral dimension of situational empathy: following the development of shared attention mechanisms, children can direct towards the intentional objects of others through embodied situational cues to perceive the psychological state of others and generate the moral empathy of "ought", leading to dyadic morality that promotes cooperative behavior. (3) The moral dimension of narrative empathy: the narrative practices of moral empathy refer to the processes by which children could perceive and understand the moral situation of characters within an embodied narrative structure, subsequently generate prosocial motives such as empathic concern, and then accept the "objective" moral norms of the group consciousness embedded in the narrative.

title: The development of cooperation and cooperative norm enforcement in children and adolescents: The role of in-group favoritism.
abstract: Various scholars have discussed the influence of group membership on cooperative behaviors in adult samples. Nonetheless, the developmental trajectories of related biases from middle childhood and early adolescence remain to be explored. Using the one-shot 4-player public goods game and inducing group membership awareness by school affiliation, we investigated the effects of group membership of imaginary partners on cooperation (Experiment 1) and cooperative norm enforcement (Experiment 2) in children and adolescents across fourth (N = 106, Mage = 9.53 years, 57 girls), sixth (N = 109, Mage = 11.46 years, 54 girls) and eighth grades (N = 102, Mage = 13.22 years, 47 girls). In Experiment 1, participants were first-party players and showed higher cooperation with in-group members (i.e., players from the same school) than out-group members (i.e., from other schools); the mediating role of cooperative expectations in in-group favoritism in cooperation was observed only among fourth and sixth graders. In Experiment 2, participants were third-party executors (i.e., could punish either in-group and out-group free-riders), and results showed that fourth and sixth graders were more lenient with in-group violators; eighth graders showed no evident bias in punishment. These findings depict a developmental pattern of decline in in-group favoritism regarding cooperation and cooperative norm enforcement from middle childhood to early adolescence. Cooperative expectations mediated the effect of group membership on cooperation only among younger students, indicating that divergent mechanisms underlie cooperative bias between groups in different grades. The discussions suggest that the understanding of norms of both cooperation and equality developed during this period.

title: The unintended negative consequences of help in childhood.
abstract: Exchanges of help in childhood produce many positive consequences: They increases academic success, promote happiness, and foster positive peer relations. For these reasons, caretakers encourage helping behavior early in life and schools implement intervention programs to nurture children's prosociality. An often-overlooked issue, however, is that providing and receiving help do not always produce positive outcomes. We review the latest research that converges to suggest that when children receive, witness, or provide help, there can be unintended negative consequences-for example, receiving help can produce feelings of incompetence. The discussion of the paper grapples with how to balance the negative and positive outcomes of helping behavior, with an eye toward promoting children's wellbeing and social cohesion in society.

title: Group Selection Promotes Prosocial Prompts in Populations of LLM Agents
abstract: Current approaches to instill prosociality in large language model (LLM) agents often rely on humans specifying desired behaviors at the individual level, which does not guarantee cooperation within LLM populations. As frontier training shifts toward individual rewards for verifiable tasks, such as mathematics and coding, this outcome-based focus may further undermine cooperation in multi-agent settings. Large-scale cooperation in human populations emerged via unguided evolutionary mechanisms, not a central architect. Group selection, in which cooperative groups within a population outcompete less cooperative ones, has been argued to be essential. In this study, we explore whether group selection can promote cooperation in populations of LLM agents. We introduce a multi-agent simulation framework in which LLM agents play a repeated social dilemma game and transmit their natural-language prompts across generations under either individual- or group-level selection. Under group selection, prompts from high-performing groups are transmitted, thereby promoting prosociality and stabilizing cooperation. Under individual selection, self-interested prompts dominate, causing populations to collapse into collective defection. This gap is robust across prompt ablations, alternative game framings, and model swaps. We theoretically reproduce key results using a replicator-mutator model, whose empirical transmission kernel predicts a phase transition at a critical threshold. Preliminary findings show that, when informed about the selection mechanism, GPT-5.4 preemptively and gradually adjusts first-generation donations. This demonstrates strong anticipatory behavior that was not observed in the other tested models. These results demonstrate that prosocial prompts and cooperative behaviors evolve in LLM agent populations under group selection.

title: Large language models replicate and predict human cooperation across experiments in game theory
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as decision-making agents in high-stakes domains and as imitators of human behavior in the social and behavioral sciences. Yet how closely LLMs mirror human decision-making remains poorly understood. This gap is critical: misalignment could produce harmful outcomes in practice, while failure to replicate human behavior renders LLMs ineffective as social simulators. Here, we address this gap by replicating large-scale game-theoretic experiments and by introducing a systematic prompting and probing framework for machine-behavioral evaluation. We test three open models typically used to power agents (Llama, Mistral, and Qwen). Across 121 dyadic games spanning four classical game types, Llama reproduces human cooperation patterns with high fidelity, while Qwen aligns closely with Nash equilibrium predictions. Characterizing models through behavioral phenotyping, we find that humans and Llama share an envious decision profile, while Qwen and Mistral exhibit different profiles. An attention-based analysis of payoff salience reveals Llama processes payoff information in a structured, layer-dependent manner absent in Qwen and Mistral, suggesting a mechanistic basis for its closer alignment with human behavior. Population-level behavioral replication is achieved without persona-based prompting, simplifying the simulation process. Extending the experimental parameter space beyond the original human-tested games, we generate and preregister testable hypotheses for novel game configurations. Our findings demonstrate appropriately configured LLMs can replicate aggregate human behavioral patterns, exhibit human-like decision phenotypes, and enable systematic exploration of unexplored experimental spaces, offering a complementary approach to traditional behavioral research that generates new empirical predictions about human social decision-making.

title: Health Dataspace Technology Acceptance Model (HDS-TAM): Development and Case Evaluation Study of Patient Acceptance of Germany's Electronic Patient Record.
abstract: The European Health Dataspace (EHDS) expands health data sharing beyond direct care and introduces governance, transparency, trust, and secondary-use considerations that are not fully captured by established technology acceptance models such as the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). To address this gap, we developed the health dataspace technology acceptance model (HDS-TAM) and evaluated it using the German electronic patient record (ePA) as an illustrative health dataspace (HDS) application. This study aimed (1) to derive an HDS-oriented technology acceptance framework from the literature and (2) to assess its applicability in explaining acceptance of the ePA from a patient perspective. A structured literature review screened 1788 records, reviewed 134 full-text papers, and retained 68 studies for model development. HDS-TAM was subsequently applied in a scenario-based online survey conducted between March and April 2025. Of 235 questionnaire accesses and 163 submitted responses, 149 valid responses were analyzed. Data were analyzed using multiple imputation, exploratory factor analysis, and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The association between behavioral intention and actual ePA use was examined using logistic regression. The model explained 75.9% of the variance in behavioral intention to use (BI, PU showed the strongest association with behavioral intention in the ePA case evaluation, while transparency and PN were mainly associated with behavioral intention through indirect pathways. The findings suggest potential value in extending traditional acceptance models with governance-related constructs relevant to HDSs. However, the severe overlap between PU and behavioral intention, low actual ePA uptake, and the young, highly educated convenience sample limit confidence in the magnitude and distinctiveness of the observed effects. HDS-TAM should therefore be regarded as a promising but preliminary framework requiring further refinement and validation.

title: The relationship of the source of punishment and personality traits with investment and punishment in a public goods game
abstract: In this study, we investigated the motivations behind punishing individuals who exploit common resources, a phenomenon crucial for resource preservation. While some researchers suggest punishment stems from concern for the common good, others propose it is driven by anger toward free riders. To probe these motivations, we developed a modified public goods game in which participants had the option to use their own money or the money from the common pool to punish free riders. The analysis included choice behavior, mouse trajectories, and personality traits like anger, empathy, and altruism. According to our results, investments were highest, and punishment was strongest if participants could punish using credits from the common pool, indicating that this is the preferred option to diminish free riding and maintain cooperation in public goods and common good contexts. Also, punishment was highest if the punisher's own investment was high, and the investment of others was low. Concerning traits, highly altruistic individuals tended to invest more and punish less in general but gave harsher punishments when they did choose to use the common pool punitively. Conversely, trait anger and trait empathy were linked to low investment while trait empathy also tended to be related to lower punishment. Taken together, these findings underscore the role of situational factors and personality traits in fostering cooperative behavior and shaping societal norms around costly punishment.

title: Psychological richness and wisdom among Filipino university students
abstract: Introduction: Psychological richness has recently been proposed as a third pathway to well-being, alongside hedonic and eudaimonic well-being. Although psychological richness has been theoretically linked to wisdom, empirical studies using an established multidimensional measure of wisdom remain limited, particularly outside predominantly Western contexts. Materials and methods: This cross-sectional study examined associations between psychological richness, wisdom, and strengths use among 201 Filipino university students. Participants completed measures of psychological richness, wisdom, openness to experience, and strengths use. Multiple regression analyses adjusted for openness to experience, age, gender, short trips, study abroad, and childhood fiction reading, with bootstrap inference based on 1000 samples. Results: Psychological richness was positively associated with overall wisdom. Specifically, psychological richness was significantly associated with acceptance of divergent perspectives, emotional regulation, prosocial behavior, social advising, and spirituality, but was not significantly associated with decisiveness and self-reflection. In addition, strengths use was positively associated with psychological richness. Conclusions: These findings provide empirical support for the association between psychological richness and wisdom. Furthermore, the findings indicate a positive association between strengths use and psychological richness. By providing evidence from a Filipino university sample, this study extends the empirical examination of psychological richness beyond the predominantly Western contexts represented in previous research.

title: How to define and promote flourishing in children in the context of early childhood education and care
abstract: This scoping review maps key constructs of child flourishing, examines their conceptualization and measurement, and synthesizes their associations with developmental outcomes. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases. Studies were screened using predefined criteria, focusing on individual-level positive psychological resources (e.g., subjective wellbeing, gratitude, hope, character strengths, resilience, and self-efficacy) and children's experiences within the Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) context with positive education. In total, 68 studies were included in the final review. Data were charted and synthesized narratively. Evidence suggests that these constructs demonstrate generally stable development across early childhood and are associated with positive outcomes, including social-emotional competence, prosocial behavior, and learning engagement. Partial support was found for the broaden-and-built theory and the undoing hypothesis. Measurement approaches varied considerably across studies, with a lack of consistent, standardized instruments and limited evidence on the developmental trajectories of these constructs. Children's experiences in ECEC, particularly character education through art, resilience projects through teamwork and mindfulness, emerged as integral to flourishing and interacted with psychological resources. Greater conceptual clarity, standardized measures, and inclusive, theory-driven research are needed to advance the field.

title: Pangenomics as a framework for discovering structural variants underlying cold tolerance in chilli pepper.
abstract: Pangenomics-based structural variant discovery offers a transformative framework to resolve missing cold-tolerance heritability in chilli pepper and accelerate climate-resilient cultivar development. Chilli pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) is a globally important crop severely restricted by cold sensitivity. SNP-based GWAS explain only 20-30% of the variance in cold tolerance, leaving a "missing heritability" gap. The GanZi/XianSheng paradox cultivars sharing >99% coding sequence identity yet exhibiting 5-10-fold differences in cold tolerance strongly implicates regulatory and dosage-based structural variants (SVs) as the primary drivers of phenotypic variation, a gap that pangenomics is positioned to address. This review synthesizes pangenomics, structural variant discovery, QTL mapping, and genome editing as an integrated framework for developing cold-tolerant chilli pepper cultivars. Based on cross-species evidence from rice, barley, and tomato pangenome studies, we propose four SV mechanisms predicted to underlie the GanZi cold-tolerance advantage: (1) regulatory SVs in promoters of CaMYB80, CBF/DREB (DREB, Dehydration-Responsive Element-Binding protein), and CaICE1; (2) copy number variations (CNVs) in antioxidant gene families (CaSOD (Superoxide Dismutase), CaCAT (Catalase), CaAPX (Ascorbate Peroxidase)) and the chlorophyll biosynthesis gene CaALAD (δ-Aminolevulinic Acid Dehydratase); (3) transposable element insertions creating novel regulatory elements in osmolyte biosynthesis genes (P5CS (Δ1-Pyrroline-5-Carboxylate Synthase), BADH (Betaine Aldehyde Dehydrogenase)); and (4) chromosomal inversions coordinating master cold-regulator gene clusters. A multi-SV haplotype in GanZi is predicted to explain 60-80% of phenotypic variance in cold tolerance, more than three times the explanatory power of SNP-based approaches. We outline a pangenome construction strategy (15-17 genomes, PacBio/Nanopore long-read sequencing, 18-24 months, $650K-$980K) followed by SV-GWAS on 200-500 accessions to identify 10-25 high-impact SVs. A four-phase breeding roadmap integrates QTL identification (1-2 years), candidate gene discovery via fine mapping and VIGS (1.5-2 years), CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing via TSWV/TRV viral vectors achieving 6.3-77.9% heritable editing efficiency (2-3 years), and multi-environment field validation across 4-6 locations (2-3 years).This integrated pangenomics-to-breeding strategy is projected to deliver climate-resilient chilli pepper cultivars with 2-5°C improvements in freezing tolerance within 7-10 years, substantially outpacing the 10-12-year timeline of traditional breeding. The proposed structural variant mechanisms remain to be experimentally confirmed in pepper and represent a testable research agenda for the chilli pepper genomics community.

title: Pharmacogenomics in Cancer Treatment: Challenges and Opportunities in African Settings.
abstract: Cancer incidence in Africa is projected to reach 2.1 million new cases annually by 2040. Current treatment guidelines remain largely based on pharmacogenomic data predominantly from European and Asian genetic profiles, potentially compromising safety and efficacy in African patients. However, limited clinical validation data, extreme intra-population genetic diversity, and significant healthcare infrastructure barriers constrain the translational application of pharmacogenomics in Africa. This review critically examines pharmacogenomic variants with established clinical actionability in cancer treatment, focusing on those with differential frequencies or African-specific alleles, and evaluates the evidence base for their implementation in African healthcare settings. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, PharmGKB, dbSNP, and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed studies reporting pharmacogenomic variants in African or African-ancestry populations relevant to cancer therapeutics. We synthesised evidence from recent African and global studies on pharmacogenomic variants affecting commonly used chemotherapy agents. Several variants show marked frequency differences between African-ancestry reference populations and European populations, including DPYD rs115232898 (2.06% vs. 0.00%), CYP2D6*17 (18.76% vs. 0%), and CYP3A5*6 (12.82% vs. 0%). However, many of these estimates derive primarily from African-American datasets and should not be interpreted as representative of continental African populations. African-specific variants such as CYP2D6*17 and DPYD rs115232898 are underrepresented in guideline development datasets. Intra-African genetic diversity is the highest globally, with Khoi-San populations harbouring extensive private variation, suggesting that no single pharmacogenomic panel will be universally applicable across the continent. While pharmacogenomics holds substantial promise for personalising cancer treatment in Africa, its current translational readiness is limited by a critical lack of African-specific clinical validation data. Priorities include multi-site validation studies, development of African-enriched genotyping panels, and integration of pharmacogenomic education into oncology practice. Implementation must be accompanied by ethical frameworks ensuring data sovereignty and equitable benefit-sharing.

title: Grandma's House: A Community-Led Partnership With University Researchers Drawing on Cultural Heritage Approaches to Support Research Development.
abstract: In African-Caribbean culture, the grandmother occupies a central moral and social position, a matriarch. In the context of community engagement, this imagery serves as a metaphor for relational and cultural intelligence in partnerships. At the suggestion of local community members, we sought to leverage this to form a community research partnership. We describe, critically review and outline the key learning points from the first year of delivering Grandma's House. The extended appreciative inquiry cycle (Define, Discover, Dream, Design and Destiny) was used to co-produce Grandma's House. Each stage was explored through meetings and workshops with community members to support the delivery of pilot events. The approach was continuously evaluated through event feedback and a final broad stakeholder meeting, where a review and SWOT analysis were conducted. Grandma's House successfully replicated the traditional African-Caribbean generation-to-generation support model. Five pilot events were successfully delivered in a range of local community settings. Key strengths were identified as collective learning and knowledge sharing; active community engagement through heritage; and building community-university relationships. Weaknesses included the challenge of funding and university inflexibility to align with community preferences. We successfully implemented a unique approach to facilitate a critical shift in the role of community members in leading collaborations in health research and practice. Grandma's House worked because it came from the community, beginning with cultural pride rather than community need. The public were the originators and drivers of this project, involved in every aspect and leading the majority. They supported the design, implementation, reflections and manuscript writing.

title: Japanese women surgeons-Past, present, and future.
abstract: Japan presents a unique cultural and medical context. While the number of male surgeons across various surgical fields declined significantly from 2014 to 2022, the number of women surgeons rose rapidly during the same period. Japanese surgeons typically face long working hours and low pay. Women surgeons also perform fewer operations, particularly high-difficulty surgeries, but handle more high-risk patients, whereas short-term outcomes show no surgeon gender differences. The 2024 work style reform for physicians capped overtime duties up to 1,860 hours per year, but the definition of "work" remains ambiguous. Generational attitudes toward domestic work are shifting; 76% of surgeons, regardless of gender, in their 20s accept sharing household chores, and more surgeons are choosing work with fewer responsibilities. The increase in women surgeons is encouraging amidst the overall decline. Work style reforms are crucial to ensure women overcome barriers like child rearing to thrive. Surgical societies are actively promoting gender equality and increasing the appointment of women to decision-making bodies. Increasing women in leadership must be fair and transparent. Indispensable leadership training for younger generations is required to effectively voice the opinions they represent.

title: Toddlers' preference for social scenes and its relation to later social-communicative skills.
abstract: Early preference for social scenes is considered a foundational precursor to social-communicative development, yet little is known about how this preference changes across toddlerhood and whether its development is related to later outcomes. This study examined the developmental changes of preference for social scenes across individuals and its longitudinal predictive effects on toddler development. A total of 61 toddlers were assessed at 12, 18, and 24 months of age. Preference for social scenes was measured at 12 and 18 months using a preferential looking paradigm, in which toddlers' spontaneous visual attention to social versus non-social stimuli was recorded using an eye tracker. General developmental outcomes were assessed at 18 and 24 months using the Ages and Stages Questionnaire-Third Edition (ASQ-3). Three key findings emerged: (1) Preference for social scenes increased over time only among toddlers who showed relatively low social preference at 12 months, revealing different developmental changes across individuals; (2) Toddlers with higher social preferential looking at 12 months demonstrated better developmental outcomes at 24 months; (3) Greater intra-individual increases in social preferential looking from 12 to 18 months were associated with more advanced development from 18 to 24 months, especially in the social and communication domains. These findings reveal that early social preferential looking follows different developmental change patterns and that intra-individual change-rather than static measurement alone-is a meaningful predictor of social-communicative development, highlighting the value of longitudinal assessment in infancy research.

title: Asymmetric dual-process mechanisms under symbolic exposure: music-induced destination perception.
abstract: Music connects listeners with places through imagery, cultural meanings, and personal associations. How cognitive and emotional responses relate to place attachment and behavioral intentions in destination-song contexts remains unclear. This study examines cognitive-affective pathway differences and the relational role of place attachment. A mixed-methods design combined Latent Dirichlet Allocation analysis of 57,228 NetEase Cloud Music comments on 15 destination-related songs with a survey of 472 respondents. Expert interpretation and psychological theory informed construct development. PLS-SEM assessed direct and indirect associations, with 5,000 paired bootstrap resamples used for exploratory pathway comparisons. Place imagery, local cultural meaning, and associative experience were positively associated with cognitive evaluation and emotional experience. Pathway comparisons showed stronger associations between place imagery and cognitive evaluation, and between associative experience and emotional experience. Cognitive-affective differences in paths to attachment, visit intention, and sharing intention were not significant. Place attachment partially mediated the associations of cognitive evaluation (β = 0.040, 95% CI [0.016, 0.072]) and emotional experience (β = 0.050, 95% CI [0.021, 0.086]) with visit intention. The findings refine the SOR framework by locating asymmetry in selected antecedent pathways and identifying place attachment as a shared relational link to visit intention. The cross-sectional design and predominance of previous visitors limit conclusions about causal ordering and new attachment formation.

title: Examining the impact of attentional focus and partner gaze on interpersonal coordination.
abstract: As a foundation of social interaction, interpersonal coordination is boosted in prosocial contexts but undermined by negative situations. Exactly how social factors shape coordination is, however, unknown. Previous literature demonstrates that for coordination to emerge people must attend to their interaction partners. This evidence, however, draws from sterile laboratory studies employing heavy-handed manipulations of little interpersonal relevance. By contrast, in more naturalistic contexts subtle differences in how people attend to themselves and others (e.g., a lingering glance vs. a suspicious side glance) can profoundly change the course of interaction. Understanding how social factors shape interpersonal coordination therefore requires consideration of aspects of attentional behaviour that better characterise everyday interaction. To this end, the current research employed virtual reality (VR) to explore how two core features of social attention, focus (self vs. other) and partner gaze (direct vs. averted), influence the spontaneous coordination of arm and head movements. The results indicated that: (i) coordination was enhanced in the other (cf. self) focus condition; and (ii) coordination was diminished in the averted (cf. direct) gaze condition. These findings provide novel evidence to indicate that the emergence of interpersonal coordination varies as a function of the everyday attentional behaviours that punctuate naturalistic social exchange. Of broad theoretical note, here we demonstrate that the among the factors constraining interpersonal coordination, the distribution of attention between self and other plays a meaningful role.

title: Evaluations of aggressive chasing interactions by 7‐month‐old infants
abstract: Recent theories of socio-moral development assume that humans evolved a capacity to evaluate others' social actions in different kinds of interactions. Prior infant studies found both reaching and visual preferences for the prosocial over the antisocial agents. However, whether the attribution of either positive or negative valence to agents' actions involved in an aggressive chasing interaction can be inferred by both reaching behaviors and visual attention deployment (i.e., disengagement of visual attention) is still an open question. Here we presented 7-month-old infants (N = 92) with events displaying an aggressive chasing interaction. By using preferential reaching and an attentional task (i.e., overlap paradigm), we assessed whether and how infants evaluate aggressive chasing interactions. The results demonstrated that young infants prefer to reach the victim over the aggressor, but neither agent affects visual attention. Moreover, such reaching preferences emerged only when dynamic cues and emotional face-like features were congruent with agents' social roles. Overall, these findings suggested that infants' evaluations of aggressive interactions are based on infants' sensitivity to some kinematic cues that characterized agents' actions and, especially, to the congruency between such motions and the face-like emotional expressions of the agents.

title: Sustainable Altruism: Simulating the Future of Prosociality and Peacebuilding—A Conceptual Review
abstract: In this article, we argue for the potential value of participatory multi-agent artificial intelligence (MAAI) modeling for addressing the pragmatic challenge of promoting a sustainable altruism among individuals and groups that will enable us to find pathways of collective action that lead toward more peaceful coexistence. Along the way, we note that this approach to modeling also addresses the scientific challenge within computer science and social simulation of creating more psychologically realistic artificial agents whose interactions occur in more realistic social networks. We identify some of the evolved cognitive and coalitional biases that make it so difficult to achieve an equilibrium of sustainable altruism in contemporary human societies, describe some of the innovative ways in which recent advances in MAAI approaches to psychological and cultural modeling open up new opportunities for simulating solutions to these challenges, and address some of the ethical issues associated with using modeling and simulating methods to help us proactively navigate the Anthropocene.

title: Interdisciplinary approach to the study of neighbourhood social cohesion and health: a new framework based on a scoping review.
abstract: We aimed to synthesise empirical evidence on neighbourhood social cohesion (NSC) to construct an interdisciplinary schematic framework. An interdisciplinary scoping review was conducted to identify the factors and outcomes related to NSC drawn from journals in sociology, psychology, public health and urban planning. A search of empirical literature was administered using PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO and Scopus for English-language studies. We included all studies that examine the role of NSC as a predictor, mediator or outcome within populations residing in Western countries. Systematic reviews or measurement studies were excluded from this review. Study characteristics, factors, outcomes and the role of NSC (eg, predictor, mediator) were extracted from 202 studies. To build the schematic framework, we aggregated all factors and outcomes into broader categories previously established by other frameworks. Connections between any two categories were labelled by whether the authors used a longitudinal design and if they attempted to establish causal evidence using a mediation analysis. The scoping review identified that NSC functions as a social determinant embedded in environmental, structural and psychosocial processes that can operate throughout the life course, interact with demographic structures and contribute to health trajectories through a network of direct and indirect pathways. Childhood exposure to high NSC was associated with developing stronger social skills and prosocial behaviour into adulthood, while exposure to low NSC increased the risk of developing anxiety, depression and substance use during adolescence. Individual resilience and self-efficacy were found to be a linking psychological mechanism between NSC and mental health. Our framework identifies NSC as a dynamic determinant of health shaped by reciprocal interactions between individuals and their neighbourhood environments. Advancing this field will require research designs that can capture these feedback processes and inform interventions aimed at reducing neighbourhood health disparities.

title: KORTİZOLÜN NÖROFİNANSAL KODLARI
abstract: İnsanların biyolojik ve psikolojik açıdan strese yanıt olarak ürettiği kortizolün etkileri, bir stres hormonu şeklinde anılmasından öte bir olgudur.Kortizole ilişkin özellikler, stres altındaki bireylerin finansal davranışlarını anlamada ve incelemede bilimsel bir araç olarak kullanılmasını mümkün kılar.Kortizolün ölçülebilir olması ve laboratuvar ortamında deneysel olarak manipüle edilebilmesi nörofinans alanında kayda değer bir imkân yaratmaktadır.Ayrıca kortizol düzeylerindeki varyasyonların karar verme mekanizmaları üzerindeki etkileri gerçekçi ve kapsamlı modeller geliştirilmesine olanak tanır.Böylece stresin finansal davranışlar üzerindeki biyolojik temelleri daha iyi anlaşılabilir ve piyasa dinamiklerine ilişkin öngörüler güçlendirilir.Bu çalışmada da kortizolün, bireylerin ekonomik ve finansal karar verme süreçlerinde, özellikle risk ve belirsizlik durumlarında nasıl rol oynadığı; ödül ve ceza öğrenme merkezli süreçlerin ya da yaklaşımın bilişsel işlevler, motivasyon ve prososyal davranışlar üzerindeki etkileri ele alınmaktadır.Nitekim beynin bu süreçlerde kritik bir biyokimyasal modülatör olduğu, kararların hızını, kalitesini ve risk algısını etkileyerek ekonomik ajanın davranışlarında dikkate değer değişikliklere yol açtığı vurgulanmaktadır.

title: Empathy, Sympathy, and Compassion: Navigating the Landscape of Emotional Resonance
abstract: Positive social interactions are crucial for our well-being. According to Fredrickson, the key to these interactions is positivity resonance, a form of positive emotional resonance that requires shared positive emotions, mutual care, and psychophysical synchrony. To achieve this, we must recognise emotions and have a fundamental ability to perceive others. Arnold’s research delves deeper into emotional reverberation, suggesting that emotional contagion arises merely from shared emotions. Empathy, sympathy, and compassion, instead, are all forms of emotional resonance that require a dynamic understanding of others’ emotions. As humans, we can interpret both our own and others’ emotional experiences, although there is some confusion between empathy and sympathy. While the two concepts may seem similar, psychologists and phenomenologists aim to clarify their essential differences. Sympathy is a positive emotion that highlights our affective consciousness and capacity for social cognition. This article argues that positive emotional resonance (Fredrickson’s notion of love) is sympathy’s psychophysiological scaffolding or counterpart. It also argues the ethical dimension of sympathy and compassion since we can foster them through moral decisions and habituation. Ultimately, it highlights the impact of sharing positive emotions on interpersonal interactions.

title: Safeguarding medical empathy and cultivating compassion in contemporary medicine
abstract: Empathy and compassion are both fundamental to patient-centred care, enhancing satisfaction, adherence and outcomes while improving clinician well-being. However, certain aspects of medical culture may put these emotional qualities at risk. The preclinical-to-clinical transition exposes students to hierarchical structures, time constraints and performance expectations prioritising technical competence over interpersonal skills. Negative role modelling, rushed consultations and inadequate emotional support normalise emotional detachment. The COVID-19 pandemic intensified burnout and moral injury, while societal desensitisation through social media compounds these effects. Although medical humanities programmes show promise, meaningful change requires addressing both curricula and clinical environments through structured reflection, compassion-focused training and recognising empathy fatigue as an occupational hazard, reaffirming medicine's ethical foundations.

title: Development and psychometric properties of the Prison Fellowship Good Citizenship Inventory (GCI): a values-based assessment for correctional settings.
abstract: This study aims to describe the development and psychometric validation of the Prison Fellowship Good Citizenship Inventory (GCI), a values-based assessment instrument designed to measure the internalization of six prosocial values (Community, Affirmation, Productivity, Restoration, Responsibility and Integrity) among prison program participants as an alternative to deficit-focused assessment approaches. Following multistage development, including item drafting, pilot testing and expert review, the GCI was administered to 559 prisoners across five state correctional facilities. Psychometric evaluation used principal axis factoring and confirmatory factor analysis to establish factor structure, with additional analyses examining internal consistency reliability, factorial invariance across gender, convergent validity (correlations with responsibility, conscientiousness and agreeableness measures) and criterion validity (associations with well-being, flourishing and criminogenic risk factors). Results supported a five-factor structure combining Responsibility and Integrity into a single dimension, with adequate internal consistency reliability (a = 0.66-0.86) across all scales. Factorial invariance testing confirmed measurement equivalence across gender groups. The GCI demonstrated significant convergent validity with established personality and responsibility measures (r = 0.42-0.57) and criterion validity through associations with human flourishing, psychological well-being and reduced antisocial characteristics, supporting the theorized relationships between prosocial values and positive outcomes. The GCI provides corrections professionals with a psychometrically sound, strengths-based assessment tool that evaluates program effectiveness beyond traditional recidivism metrics by measuring positive value development. This values-based approach offers a theoretically grounded alternative to risk-focused assessment models, aligning with emerging research on strength-based rehabilitation and desistance-focused interventions in correctional settings.

title: Protocol for an agent-based model of recombination in bacteria playing a public goods game.
abstract: Agent-based models are composed of individual agents coded for traits, such as cooperation and cheating, that interact in a virtual world based on defined rules. Here, we describe the use of an agent-based model of homologous recombination in bacteria playing a public goods game. We describe steps for software installation, setting model parameters, running and testing models, and visualization and statistical analysis. This protocol is useful in analyses of horizontal gene transfer, bacterial sociobiology, and game theory. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Lee et al.

title: The effect of cultural socialization on the development of prosocial behavior and academic performance in young adults
abstract: Socialization is a lifelong process of learning that influences an individual’s attitude, behavior, and values. The term “cultural socialization" specifically refers to the learning mechanism by which young adults attain cultural maturity by acquiring awareness of their cultural group values, resulting in the development of a sense of belonging toward that particular cultural group. Family as an agent of socialization plays a crucial role in imparting cultural traits and values to its members, which varies from one family to another due to cultural diversity and social change. The significant influence of peer groups, in addition to family, as a socializing entity adds complexity to this learning system and makes it a potential source for creating distinctions and fostering the development of superiority and inferiority complexes among the members. Young adults who experience socialization from both entities encounter a chaotic state of mind that impacts their behavior and academic performance. Hence, this study seeks to comprehend the significance of cultural socialization in the development of prosocial behavior and academic achievement within diverse cultural contexts, such as educational institutions. The study adopted a quantitative methodology with simple random sampling administered through a questionnaire. The findings show that cultural socialization has a potential influence on academic performance and prosocial behavior. Thus, cultural socialization serves as a catalyst for enhancing prosocial behavior, subsequently leading to better academic performance.

title: Concevoir des esprits sociaux : Comment le design de l'IA et les normes de communication façonnent la perception, l'engagement et le comportement prosocial des humains
abstract: L'importance des agents conversationnels numériques a récemment augmenté, de nombreuses entreprises adoptant des agents pilotés par l'IA pour gérer les demandes d'affaires et faciliter les interactions quotidiennes avec les clients. Étant donné la réticence générale des individus envers l'IA, certaines entreprises choisissent d'anthropomorphiser leurs bots de service client (par exemple, en leur donnant des noms et des avatars). Cependant, l'efficacité de ces pratiques n'est pas claire dans le cas des voicebots (c'est-à-dire, des bots conversationnels basés sur la voix), car ces interventions ne sont pas axées sur la voix. Nous nous concentrons sur la voix, en tant que caractéristique clé des voicebots, et proposons une approche d'anthropomorphisme axée sur la voix. À travers une série de cinq expériences, nous démontrons le rôle de l'attribution d'un accent au voicebot sur les perceptions anthropomorphiques et l'engagement ultérieur des utilisateurs. Plus précisément, nous montrons que les utilisateurs ont une préférence plus marquée pour interagir avec des voicebots et adoptent des attitudes plus positives envers eux lorsque ces voicebots sont équipés d'accents étrangers. Nous mettons en lumière le rôle sous-jacent des perceptions anthropomorphiques en tant que mécanisme psychologique, suggérant que les accents étrangers servent de cue anthropomorphique crucial, influençant l'attitude des utilisateurs et entraînant une préférence pour les voicebots par rapport aux agents en direct. Ces résultats fournissent des éclairages pour les entreprises cherchant à améliorer l'engagement client grâce à leur voicebot, ainsi que pour les entreprises impliquées dans le développement des technologies voicebot

title: Innovation Management in Medical Education: A Narrative Review of Its Organizational Dimensions, Facilitators, and Barriers.
abstract: Innovation has become increasingly important in medical education; however, successful innovation requires more than the adoption of individual educational interventions or technologies. Institutions need organizational capabilities that enable innovation to be developed, implemented, sustained, and evaluated. Despite growing interest in educational innovation, evidence regarding how medical education institutions manage innovation at the organizational level remains fragmented. This narrative review aimed to synthesize evidence on the organizational dimensions, facilitators, and barriers influencing innovation management in medical education and to develop a comprehensive understanding of how institutions create conditions for sustainable innovation. A narrative review approach was used. Literature was identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Magiran, and Google Scholar, complemented by reference list checking and limited citation tracking of relevant publications. Database searches targeted publications from 2019 to 2026, while additional conceptually important studies identified through supplementary approaches were considered. Evidence was synthesized according to six organizational dimensions: leadership, governance, and innovation policy; human capital development and empowerment; organizational culture and climate; knowledge management and innovation infrastructure; change management, implementation, and sustainability; and evaluation, quality improvement, and social accountability. The reviewed evidence indicates that innovation management in medical education is a multidimensional institutional process rather than an isolated activity. Leadership commitment, supportive governance structures, faculty development, empowerment, innovation-oriented organizational cultures, knowledge-sharing systems, implementation capacity, and continuous evaluation emerged as interconnected factors influencing innovation sustainability. Major barriers included organizational resistance, limited resources, fragmented governance, insufficient institutional readiness, and challenges in maintaining innovations beyond initial implementation phases. Innovation management in medical education should be approached as an institutional capability requiring alignment among leadership, organizational structures, human capacity, cultural conditions, implementation processes, and evaluation mechanisms, rather than reliance on isolated innovation activities. Future research should move beyond individual innovation projects toward longitudinal and comparative investigations of how medical education institutions develop and sustain innovation capacity over time.

title: Linac performance benchmarking: Feasibility of a web-based tool for comparison of local machine performance check (MPC) results with the global community.
abstract: Varian machine performance check (MPC) is a manufacturer integrated quality control system included as standard for TrueBeam and Halcyon linear accelerators (linacs) to assess performance using a broad range of geometric and beam tests. MPC is a highly standardized method of performance testing, is generally free of inter-user variability and is quick and easy to perform allowing daily acquisitions. Therefore, previous studies have highlighted the potential of comparative analysis of MPC data in investigating differences in performance of individual linacs and identifying outliers. Statistical process control (SPC) is an established approach commonly used to assess stability and behavior of sequential data and identify standard operating ranges which has previously been applied to radiotherapy quality assurance data and MPC data. This study aimed to investigate the feasibility of a web-based platform using SPC and aggregated MPC data to allow users to compare their machine performance against that of a cohort of others in the radiotherapy community. A previously developed web-based platform for radiotherapy data sharing was expanded to include the MPC data collection and comparison tool. Pilot centers exported data from their MPC applications and uploaded it through center-specific portals. Within the application, SPC analysis was used to calculate upper control limits (UCL), lower control limits (LCL) and central lines (CL) for the data sets of each individual linac as well as cohort averages. Interactive plots of longitudinal data for individual machines were displayed for users and overlaid with SPC limits for the specific machine and the cohort averages. Additional analyses were conducted externally from the app where the average and range of SPC control limits for the cohort were compared against MPC tolerances. MPC data for 57 648 measurements taken between April 2016 and May 2026 were collected across seven centers from 21 TrueBeam linacs (15 with Millennium multi-leaf collimator (MLC), six with HD120 MLCs) and one Halcyon. Variation in performance for specific tests was identified for individual machines compared against the cohort as well as for individual MLC leaves for specific machines. Across the cohort of TrueBeam linacs, average control ranges for all geometric tests were within MPC thresholds. However, the range of values for UCL and LCL exceeded tolerances for relative gantry angle. Machines installed before 2021 were found to have slightly larger variability in mean MLC offset with an average control range width of 0.20 mm and 0.18 mm for bank A and B, respectively, compared to machines installed after 2021 of 0.10 mm and 0.13 mm. Analysis of data for individual linacs segmented per year showed a change in mean MLC offset occurring around 2021. The usefulness and feasibility of a tool to compare MPC data against the radiotherapy community was demonstrated. Inter-center comparison of data allowed trends to be identified which would otherwise not be observable for individual centers. Further development and distribution of the MPC data sharing and comparison tool may provide improved confidence and understanding of machine performance and assist low-resourced clinics in delivering safe and accurate radiotherapy treatments.

title: Flight Physician Training and Workforce Sustainability Within an Integrated Emergency Department-Intensive Care Unit-Helicopter Emergency Medical Services Staffing Model: A Rural Helicopter Emergency Medical Services Experience in Japan.
abstract: Maintaining physician-staffed helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS) in rural regions is increasingly challenging because of physician shortages, workforce sustainability concerns, and limited opportunities for dedicated flight physician staffing. We developed an integrated staffing and training model in which emergency physicians collectively provide emergency department (ED), intensive care unit (ICU), pediatric emergency, and HEMS care while participating in a regional physician-sharing collaboration. This single-center retrospective study evaluated all consecutive HEMS missions conducted between April 2021 and March 2026 at a rural tertiary emergency and critical care center in Japan. Flight physician training was conducted through on-the-job training (OJT) embedded within routine ED, ICU, pediatric emergency, and HEMS practices. Missions performed during supervised OJT were compared with those performed after independent certification. Operational performance was assessed using on-scene time, scene intervention rates, intubation rates, cardiopulmonary resuscitation rates, and hospital mortality. Six physicians completed training; 4 achieved independent practice within 6 months and 2 within 12 months. The average annual flight volume was approximately 30 missions per physician. A total of 189 missions were analyzed. Patient characteristics were comparable between 98 OJT and 91 independent missions. No differences were observed across operational performance measures; no procedural, medication, or operational incidents occurred. Despite relatively limited individual flight exposure, most trainees achieved independent practice within 6 months, and operational performance following certification was not inferior to that of supervised training. Integrated acute care practice may support the development and maintenance of flight physician competency in resource-limited rural environments.

title: Distinct Localization of Leishmania tarentolae and Trypanosoma platydactyli in the Putative Natural Vector Sergentomyia minuta: Does This Reflect Co-evolution?
abstract: Leishmania tarentolae and Trypanosoma platydactyli are reptile parasites that naturally share the same vertebrate hosts and are presumed to be transmitted by the sand fly Sergentomyia minuta. Despite their long-recognized association, the development of T. platydactyli in its most probable natural vector has remained largely unknown, and the interactions of both parasites during co-infection have not been investigated. Here, we experimentally infected laboratory-reared S. minuta by xenodiagnoses on naturally infected Tarentola mauritanica geckos carrying either single or mixed infections. Parasite species were distinguished using species-specific PCRs, and their localization, infection dynamics, and morphological development were examined by light microscopy and morphometric analyses. Leishmania tarentolae predominantly colonized the Malpighian tubules, whereas T. platydactyli exhibited a suprapylarian development, consistently colonizing the abdominal and thoracic midguts, and frequently reaching the cardia and the stomodeal valve. During development, T. platydactyli underwent a transition from epimastigotes to paramastigotes and trypomastigotes, with the latter becoming the predominant late-stage form that likely represents the transmissible stage. In contrast, L. tarentolae maintained the characteristic developmental pattern previously described for the subgenus Sauroleishmania, with short and long promastigotes predominating throughout development and metacyclic promastigotes appearing during late infections. Our findings provide the first comprehensive description of the development of T. platydactyli in S. minuta and demonstrate distinct tissue tropisms between the two trypanosomatids sharing the same vertebrate host and insect vector. These results support the hypothesis that long-term co-evolution has driven niche partitioning within the sand fly, allowing both parasites to coexist while potentially employing distinct transmission strategies.

title: Why Can Cross-End Point Transfer Fail in Computational Toxicology? Diagnosing Decision-Structure Incompatibility across 13 End Points under Scaffold-Held-Out Evaluation.
abstract: Cross-end point information sharing may improve toxicity prediction when labeled data are limited, but biologically related end points are not necessarily predictively compatible. We evaluated transfer strategies across 13 toxicity end points using scaffold-disjoint repeated cross-validation with strict leakage control. The benchmark compared data-level pooling with higher-level approaches, including stacking, multitask learning, model-agnostic meta-learning, and frozen-encoder feature augmentation (FEFA). Direct cross-prediction between different end points was generally weak, with a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.525 across 156 ordered end point pairs, indicating limited standalone portability of end point-specific decision rules. Global data merging reduced macro-average ROC-AUC by 0.0287 relative to end point-specific baselines, whereas several higher-level approaches produced modest gains. The strongest macro-average improvements were observed for stacking (+0.0101 ROC-AUC) and FEFA (+0.0070), although effects varied substantially among end points. Additional decision-structure and representation analyses were consistent with transfer performance being strategy- and target-dependent rather than determined by biological relatedness alone. These findings support leakage-controlled, end point-specific evaluation when using cross-end point learning for chemical toxicity assessment and caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous toxicity data.

title: [Green Development Performance Evaluation and Differentiation Improvement Strategy in the Yangtze River Delta Region: Based on the Synergistic Perspective of Carbon Reduction， Pollution Reduction， and Green Expansion].
abstract: Green development is a key strategy to promote the modernization of our ecological and environmental governance system and realize the comprehensive transformation of the economy and society. Based on the input-output framework， a green development performance evaluation system is constructed from the perspective of carbon reduction， pollution reduction， and green growth synergy， and the green development performance of 27 cities in the Yangtze River Delta Region from 2012 to 2023 is measured by using the super-efficient SBM model. The spatio-temporal evolution law is also analyzed by combining kernel density estimation and the Dagum Gini coefficient decomposition method. The results show that： ① During the study period， the overall green development performance of the Yangtze River Delta Region showed a trend of "first decreasing and then rising，" with the average fluctuating from 0.598 to 0.877， an increase of 46.66%. ② At the provincial level， Zhejiang and Anhui had obvious performance advantages at the beginning of the study period， but the improvement rate was slow， while the green development performance of Shanghai and Jiangsu increased significantly during the study period. At the city level， the green development level of six cities including Shaoxing and Chizhou has always been at the forefront of efficiency， with Wuxi， Changzhou， Suzhou， Jiaxing， and other cities increasing the most， while the green development performance of Tongling and Wuhu in Anhui has declined. ③ The intercity differences in green development performance in the Yangtze River Delta Region eased during the study period， and the overall Gini coefficient decreased from 0.248 to 0.125， of which intra-provincial differences were the main source of the overall differences. Based on the empirical results， a four-quadrant diagram is constructed from the two dimensions of economic development level and green development performance； the differentiated paths for performance improvement in different cities are proposed； and a green collaborative guarantee mechanism is proposed from the aspects of policy coordination， industrial collaboration， ecological joint governance， and science and technology sharing.

title: Naxos disease: current insights from early clinical observations to genetics and precision medicine.
abstract: Naxos disease is the prototype of the Naxos disease cardiocutaneous spectrum, a group of inherited desmosomal disorders characterised by distinctive hair and skin abnormalities that precede the development of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM). Since its original clinical description in 1986 and the subsequent identification of the first ACM-causing gene (JUP), Naxos disease has provided fundamental insights into the pathogenesis, diagnosis and management of inherited desmosomal cardiomyopathies. This review provides current insights into the evolving clinical spectrum, encompassing the characteristic cutaneous signature, early electrical abnormalities, progressive structural myocardial remodelling, inflammatory ("hot-phase") episodes, ventricular arrhythmias and heart failure. We discuss the expanding genotype-phenotype relationships involving JUP, DSP and DSC2, highlighting how distinct genetic substrates influence ventricular involvement, disease severity and clinical outcomes while sharing common desmosomal mechanisms. Particular emphasis is placed on early clinical recognition, multimodality imaging, genetic diagnosis, risk stratification and lifelong multidisciplinary management. Finally, we discuss the emerging role of international collaborative registries, including NAXCARE, in generating prospective real-world evidence to refine genotype-informed surveillance, improve risk prediction and support precision medicine. Nearly four decades after its original description, Naxos disease has evolved from a rare inherited syndrome into the prototype of desmosomal cardiomyopathy, demonstrating how careful clinical observation can drive molecular discovery, precision medicine and improved patient care.

title: Zfpm1 regulates endothelial-mesenchymal transition and endocardial cell differentiation.
abstract: The endocardium is the endothelial component of the heart that forms valves. Endocardial (EC) cells undergo endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EndoMT) which distinguishes them from endothelial (ET) cells, despite sharing markers and a mesodermal origin. Nfatc1, uniquely labels EC cells but is not sufficient for EC cell specification, since knockouts form valves, albeit underdeveloped, therefore the regulators that specify EC fate remain incompletely defined. Using an in vivo Nfatc1 reporter system, we show that EC and ET cells are transcriptionally distinct and identify the transcription factor Zfpm1 (Fog1), as a potential regulator of EC cell specification. In an in vitro embryonic stem cell differentiation model, Zfpm1 knockdown results in an impaired EC cell differentiation, with reduced endothelial-mesenchymal transition and altered contractility and beating phenotype, consistent with reduced differentiation of EC cells affecting the crosstalk with myocardial cells. These findings are consistent with data linking mutations in the human ZFPM1 gene with non-syndromic tetralogy of Fallot. This and the broad expression pattern across all regions of the cardiac outflow tract support a role for Zfpm1 in mammalian EC cell differentiation and endothelial-mesenchymal transition. This study extends the in vivo evidence of its relevance to cardiac development and provides new insights into the transcriptional control of EC lineages.
