title: The wisdom of the diverse crowd(funders)
abstract: Crowdfunding platforms aim to democratize entrepreneurial finance by creating ecosystems that elicit the ‘wisdom of crowds’—aggregating the judgments of individual and often amateur funders. However, there is limited evidence on whether crowds can effectively apply their collective wisdom on these platforms. Our study addresses these questions by analyzing a crowdlending platform that connects Western lenders with borrowers in developing countries. We examine whether lenders effectively screen borrowers, identify platform attributes that influence lenders’ screening accuracy, and uncover the underlying mechanisms driving these effects. To achieve this, we exploit interventions by platform administrators that allow us to observe the counterfactual repayment performance of loans that failed to attract sufficient funding. Our results indicate that rowdlenders can effectively screen creditworthy borrowers, but only when financial information about borrowers is made available. Lenders’ screening effectiveness diminishes substantially for prosocial loans, as many funders converge on similar, socially motivated decisions. These findings provide novel evidence on crowdlenders' performance, highlighting key trade-offs for crowdfunding platforms and offering actionable insights for their administrators.

title: The Life-sustenance Hypothesis: Understanding Human-Nature Connection by Integrating Rousseau's Philosophy to Contemporary Systems Biological Viewpoints
abstract: This paper develops the life-sustenance hypothesis to explain the multifaceted phenomenon of the human-nature connection. It is based on an interpretation of Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s philosophy brought into contemporary times via recent multidisciplinary research and theoretical underpinnings. Rousseau suggested that humans have two innate, instinctive drives he called amour-de-soi and pitié—a self-preservative drive, and its enlargement, an inclination to help other living beings in distress. The life-sustenance hypothesis is rooted in a systems biological framework situating humans as interconnected parts within a nested system of life. Corresponding to Rousseau’s drives, this interconnectedness is suggested to give rise to the dynamics between two life-preserving orientations that guide our manners-of-being in the world: a self-sustaining and a ‘life-sustaining’ orientation shared by all organisms, albeit manifested differently. The experience of nature connectedness, along with altruistic impulses, are proposed to be human manifestations of the life-sustaining orientation. Moreover, in line with Rousseau’s philosophy, it is posited that the modern, individualistic lifestyle has given rise to an imbalance between these orientations leading to problems in prosociality, proenvironmentalism, and overall well-being. One means by which to regain balanced manners-of-being might be to enhance our nature connectedness. Possible physiological indicators for the hypothesis are explored.

title: The effect of psilocybin on empathy and prosocial behavior: a proposed mechanism for enduring antidepressant effects
abstract: Psilocybin is a serotonergic psychedelic shown to have enduring antidepressant effects. Currently, the mechanism for its enduring effects is not well understood. Empathy and prosocial behavior may be important for understanding the therapeutic benefit of psilocybin. In this article we review the effect of psilocybin on empathy and prosocial behavior. Moreover, we propose that psilocybin may induce a positive feedback loop involving empathy and prosocial behavior which helps explain the observed, enduring antidepressant effects.

title: Agent-based simulation of equity-oriented water reallocation under drought: A case study of the Geum River Basin
abstract: Study region : Geum River Basin, South Korea, a structurally heterogeneous watershed with 14 agricultural, 12 domestic/industrial intake, and 3 hydropower stakeholders. The basin has the highest agricultural water demand among South Korea’s six major river basins, with precipitation concentrated in the summer monsoon season, making dam operations critical for balancing competing water demands during irrigation. Study focus : This study develops an integrated framework to improve equitable water allocation during droughts by coupling a basin-scale allocation model with an Agent-Based Model (ABM). While centralized optimization overlooks decentralized social dynamics, autonomous stakeholder agents make voluntary diversion decisions based on locally perceived reliability deficits, redistributing water to the most vulnerable peers via hypothetical conveyance infrastructure. Streamflow is represented by SWAT-derived daily inflows spanning 39 water years (October 1981–September 2020). New hydrological insights and conclusions : First, agricultural water supply vulnerability in the Geum River Basin is governed less by absolute demand magnitude and more by basin topology and infrastructure configuration. Tributary-dominated subbasins (Agr 7, Agr 11, and Agr 13), which are structurally isolated from the regulated mainstem, exhibited the lowest supply reliability during the severe historical droughts of 1994–1997 and 2014–2017, identifying these locations as priority targets for adaptive drought management in the basin. Second, agent-based simulation of voluntary water donation among Geum River stakeholders demonstrates that equity improvements can emerge as system-level outcomes from repeated decentralized interactions. During drought period, the agricultural Gini coefficient decreased from 0.152 (no ABM) to 0.097–0.117 across three behavioral scenarios, with the largest reliability gains concentrated at the most structurally vulnerable tributary nodes. Third, sensitivity analysis across nine supply–demand combinations confirmed that the simulated equity benefit within the Geum River Basin is robust to variations in inflow magnitude and irrigation demand scaling, with gains increasing proportionally under higher demand pressure. However, the Pro-social scenario yielded diminishing equity returns relative to the Bounded Rational scenario, as excessively frequent donations reduced the reliability of intake donor stakeholders, suggesting that moderate rather than maximum cooperation produces the most balanced outcomes across stakeholder types.

title: Resolving social dilemmas with minimal reward transfer
abstract: Abstract Social dilemmas present a significant challenge in multi-agent cooperation because individuals are incentivised to behave in ways that undermine socially optimal outcomes. Consequently, self-interested agents often avoid collective behaviour. In response, we formalise social dilemmas and introduce a novel metric, the general self-interest level, to quantify the disparity between individual and group rationality in such scenarios. This metric represents the maximum proportion of their individual rewards that agents can retain while ensuring that a social welfare optimum becomes a dominant strategy. Our approach diverges from traditional concepts of altruism, instead focusing on strategic reward redistribution. By transferring rewards among agents in a manner that aligns individual and group incentives, rational agents will maximise collective welfare while pursuing their own interests. We provide an algorithm to compute efficient transfer structures for an arbitrary number of agents, and introduce novel multi-player social dilemma games to illustrate the effectiveness of our method. This work provides both a descriptive tool for analysing social dilemmas and a prescriptive solution for resolving them via efficient reward transfer contracts. Applications include mechanism design, where we can assess the impact on collaborative behaviour of modifications to models of environments.

title: Developing Empathy in Children through the Moral Lessons in Buddhist Jataka Tales
abstract: Abstract This study examines the impact of Buddhist Jataka tales, rich in compassion, kindness, and selflessness on fostering empathy in children. The study employed an exploratory quasi-experimental design using a pre-test–post-test control group approach aiming to explore the potential influence of Buddhist Jataka tales on children's empathetic behaviour in a natural classroom setting rather than to establish definitive causal conclusions. Forty-one Grade 5 students (10 years old) from a government school in Colombo participated in this exploratory pilot study. Participants were assigned to an experimental group and a control group according to the school's classroom organization. The experimental group engaged with three Buddhist Jataka stories, followed by discussions. Both groups completed questionnaires, with a follow-up, two weeks later. Results showed increased and sustained empathetic behaviour in the experimental group, suggesting that Buddhist Jataka tales can effectively support emotional and ethical development in educational settings.

title: Influences of music and rhythm on prosocial behavior in preschool children
abstract: Music has existed in human culture for at least 40,000 years and is present today in all societies. Its perception, appreciation and production are based on a set of cognitive abilities commonly referred to as "musicality." Some authors have suggested that musicality may have an evolutionary origin. Specifically, it may have evolved because music promotes social cohesion within groups. This hypothesis is supported by studies in developmental psychology, which show that joint music-making promotes empathy in 8 to 11-year-olds, as well as cooperation and helping behavior in 4-year-old children. However, many questions remain unanswered, particularly regarding the effects of music listening on social behavior (beyond joint production), the conditions under which such effects may be observed (e.g., individual versus joint listening), the musical properties and mechanisms involved (e.g., the role of rhythm and interpersonal synchronization), and the broader evolution of musicality across the living world beyond our own species. In 2017, we already demonstrated a positive influence of joint listening to classical music on social interaction in a cooperative task context in children aged 3 to 6, as well as in a parrot species, the cockatiels (suggesting convergent evolution in humans and certain birds, thus indicating a partly biological, not just cultural, origin of musicality). The study presented here focuses specifically on children but is also part of a larger comparative project involving humans, non-human primates, and birds. In the case of children, this study showed that percussive, rhythmic electronic music fostered more social interactions and cooperation among pairs of 3 to 6-year-old children compared to classical music (Mozart's Sonata K448), white noise, a "scrambled" version of the stimulus used, or silence. The role of rhythm and interpersonal synchronization will be further explored in the future by testing the influence of new stimuli listened to together or separately, with or without concurrent music production. We also plan to examine the spontaneous movements of individuals during listening and their relationship to observed behaviors in subsequent prosocial tasks.

title: Is leisure‐time reading related to empathy and social skills in 8‐ to 10‐year‐old children?
abstract: There is growing interest in the effects of reading on empathy and prosocial behaviour but not enough is known about the associations among these variables in children. In a study undertaken at a single time point, we examined children's leisure reading and self-reported prosocial behaviour, and whether the relation between them was mediated by affective or cognitive empathy or by theory of mind. We tested 113 English-speaking children aged 8-10 years from a UK primary school. Analyses showed that reading and prosocial behaviour are related, and that the relation was partly explained by variance shared with empathy, particularly affective rather than cognitive empathy. Future work focusing on causal aspects of these relations should provide further guidance on the practical implications of these results.

title: MOOD AND EMPATHY ON PROSOCIAL BEHAVIOUR AMONG MUSLIM ADOLESCENTS IN PADANG CITY
abstract: This research is motivated by the phenomenon at the Dharmabakti Nusantara Health Vocational School in Padang City; mood and empathy are thought to influence prosocial behaviour. This study aims to analyse: 1) mood, empathy and prosocial behaviour, 2) the relationship between mood and prosocial behaviour, 3) the relationship between empathy and prosocial behaviour, and 4) the relationship between mood and empathy together with prosocial behaviour. The method used in this study is a Quantitative method that aims to determine the relationship and influence between variables. The research sample was taken from the existing population of 80 students. The research instrument used a questionnaire with a Likert scale model. The data were analysed with descriptive statistics, simple regression, and multiple regression; the results of the research data analysis obtained an R-value of 0.558 with a p level = 0.000 (p <0.05). There is a significant relationship between mood and empathy with prosocial behaviour. R2 =0,311 %. This study proves a positive and meaningful relationship between philosophy and heart in prosocial behaviour at SMK Dharmabakti Nusantara Pota Padang.

title: The Relationship between Well-Being, Empathy, Moral Identity, and Spirituality on Prosocial Behavior among Malaysian Youth
abstract: This study explores the influence of well-being, empathy, moral identity, and spirituality on prosocial behavior among Malaysian youth.A quantitative approach was employed with a sample of 411 participants, using Pearson correlation and multiple regression analyses to investigate the relationships between these variables.The results revealed that moral identity was the strongest predictor of prosocial behavior, followed closely by spirituality, empathy, and well-being.These findings highlight the central role of moral identity in shaping prosocial actions, with spirituality and empathy also playing significant roles.Well-being, while slightly less influential, still contributes meaningfully to prosocial behavior by promoting emotional stability and life satisfaction.The study emphasizes the importance of fostering moral development, spiritual growth, and emotional well-being to encourage prosocial behavior in youth.Policymakers, educators, and community leaders are encouraged to implement programs that focus on these key areas to promote a more compassionate and engaged youth population.

title: Severity over source: Understanding transgressors' motive attributions of punishment
abstract: Punishment conveys social information to transgressors, who attribute motives to punishers. Drawing on the motive-attribution framework, we examined whether transgressors' attributions to competitive (i.e. harming transgressors), individualistic (i.e. managing one's own interests) and prosocial (i.e. healing relationships) motives differ depending on whether punishment is administered by victims (second-party punishment) or uninvolved observers (third-party punishment), and how these attributions relate to downstream affective, relational and behavioural outcomes. In an incentivized Stealing Game, participants could steal valuable points and were punished either by the victim or an observer. Subsequently, transgressors reported their motive attributions, affect and willingness to reconcile and completed a measure of prosocial behaviour towards an unrelated other. Contrary to predictions, motive attributions did not systematically differ between second- and third-party punishment, except that third-party punishment was more strongly attributed to reputational concerns (i.e. a subdimension of individualistic motive attribution). Punishment severity emerged as an important predictor, with harsher sanctions linked to stronger competitive and individualistic attributions. Competitive motive attribution, in turn, was associated with higher negative affect and lower positive affect, willingness to reconcile and prosocial behaviour. Overall, transgressors' responses to punishment were less clearly shaped by who punished and more closely linked to punishment severity and motive attribution.

title: The Role of the Effectiveness of Mosque Social Activities and Their Consistency in Repetition Donation Decisions (Case Study of Masjid Raya Al Insan)
abstract: Mosques play a vital role in Islam, serving not only as places of worship but also as centers for various social activities and economic empowerment, including the collection of social funds such as zakat, infaq, and sadaqah (charity). However, data from the 2024 Mosque Information System (SIMAS) of the Ministry of Religious Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia shows that of the total 694,725 mosques and prayer rooms, only 28,138 have a Mosque Welfare Agency (BKM), indicating that the majority of mosque management remains traditional and has not adopted modern management. Masjid Raya Al Insan (MRAI) in Kebayoran Lama, South Jakarta, is known for frequently holding social and humanitarian activities, both routine and incidental, for the congregation and the community living around the mosque. Previous research has examined factors such as transparency, accountability, the attitude of mosque management, and the social and religious influences of donors on trust and donation decisions. However, there is still little research that specifically examines the role of the effectiveness of mosque social activities and their consistency on repeat donation decisions. Using a qualitative case study method through in-depth interviews with administrators and donors, this study evaluates the role of the effectiveness and consistency of MRAI's social programs on repeat donations. The results show that the effectiveness of social activities is assessed by the emotional impact and tangible solutions for the community, not simply by statistical figures. It was found that repeat donation decisions are driven by a strong synergy between theological motivation and trust in the integrity of the administrators. Specifically, the consistency of social programs proved to be a key factor in building donor loyalty, validating the paradigm that "busy mosques" that actively distribute funds actually attract more donations. The study concluded that program consistency creates a sense of security and inner satisfaction for donors. As a recommendation, mosque administrators need to immediately undertake digital transformation in transparent financial reporting and implement Customer Relationship Management (CRM) to maintain donor relationships to ensure the sustainability of funding for community programs.

title: Random Forest for Multi-Output Analysis of University Students' Prosocial Behaviors
abstract: This study examines differential effects that different demographic variables and the subgroup-based community management model in universities on college students' prosocial behavior. Our dataset includes survey responses from 307 students enrolled in universities implementing this management model and 200 students from non-implementing universities. We employed the Random Forest algorithm to training AI model on 90% of the participant sample and reserving the remaining 10% for validation. The model achieved a prediction accuracy of 96.08%, demonstrating strong reliability in assessing the relationship between community-based subgroup management and prosocial behavioral outcomes. Furthermore, Random Forest shows the importance of independent variables.

title: How social norms emerge: the interindividual actor-critic
abstract: Social norms shape a vast range of human behaviors, from everyday interactions to major life choices. Yet, existing theories of norm emergence typically focus either on why certain norms arise (substantive properties) or on how they spread and persist (dynamical properties), often making conflicting assumptions. Here, we propose a unified account in which norms prescribing how one ought to act emerge naturally from the fundamental algorithms that guide learning—whether in social or non-social settings. Our account builds on recent advances in decision-making and emotion research that have highlighted ‘actor-critic’ models as a core mechanism of learning from feedback. We extend this mechanism to social settings by assuming that it is not only we who critique our actions, others critique our actions as well. By simulating this interindividual form of learning, we show that it uniquely produces group behavior that exhibits both substantive and dynamical properties of real-world social norms, including prosociality, ingroup bias, stickiness, S-shaped curves, and local conformity / global diversity. Our framework thus offers a uniquely parsimonious way to bridge the gap between individual learning and group behavior.

title: What leads employees to hide knowledge: a review of theoretical underpinnings
abstract: Purpose Given the detrimental impact of knowledge hiding (KH) on contemporary organizations, it is crucial to investigate its determinants. This paper aims to identify the theoretical underpinnings of determinants of KH and discuss the findings in a broader systems and cybernetic perspective. The paper presents a promising agenda to advance theoretical research on KH determinants. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review of studies published over the past decade was conducted to identify and categorize the main theoretical perspectives underpinning KH drivers. Findings Research on KH determinants largely focuses on internal organizational factors and is grounded in social-based theories, conservation of resources (COR) theory, and psychological ownership (PO) theory. Social-based theories view KH as reciprocal behavior, COR frames it as a defensive response to resource loss, and PO positions it as a means of protecting owned knowledge. Recent studies also highlight the influence of individual differences and emotions. However, external and contextual factors remain underexplored. Originality/value This study comprehensively examines the theoretical underpinnings of determinants of KH, and suggests a promising research agenda. Further, it addresses the systemic nature of KH in organizational processes.

title: Symbolic promotions: Conceptualization and empirical investigation
abstract: Abstract Symbolic promotions are an increasingly prevalent marketing practice globally, yet little is known about how or when they influence consumer behavior. We conceptualize symbolic promotions as a distinct type of sales promotion that creates value by reinforcing consumers' social identity through shared group membership rather than by providing economic incentives, such as reward-based promotions, or supporting distant others, such as cause-related marketing promotions (CMPs). We investigate the effectiveness of symbolic promotions and their underlying mechanisms using a multimethod approach. A nine-year longitudinal field study of daily sales for 22,084 books demonstrates that an existing symbolic promotion ("On August 12, I buy a Quebec book!") generates a substantial increase in sales, with stronger effects for lesser-known brands than for well-known brands. A follow-up experiment uncovers the unique mechanisms underlying these effects, showing that symbolic promotions stimulate curiosity and community rootedness, which in turn enhance multiple types of behavioral intentions, i.e., the likelihood of participating in the promotion, sharing it on social media, and future brand consideration. Together, these findings position symbolic promotions as a distinct, complementary addition to firms’ promotional portfolios, and demonstrate how firms can leverage shared identities to create value beyond traditional monetary incentives, with implications for various stakeholders.

title: Temporal Comparisons Elicit Greater Pride, Lower Shame, and Stronger Improvement Orientation Among Chinese Children.
abstract: Upward social comparisons are widely used to encourage effort, yet they often lead to negative emotions. Temporal comparisons may support self-improvement while preserving positive self-experience. This study investigates whether temporal comparisons offer these potential benefits for Chinese children. Two between-subjects experiments were conducted with Chinese primary and secondary school students (aged 8-16 years) in autumn 2024. We manipulated comparison type and comparison direction through reading-writing tasks. Study 1 (N = 632, 51% girls) used writing tasks involving comparisons with better or worse peers or past selves, alongside a no-comparison control. Study 2 added 285 participants (51% girls) who imagined and wrote about better or worse future selves, sharing the social-comparison and control groups from Study 1. After the tasks, participants reported pride, shame, improvement goals, and superiority goals. Past-self comparisons elicited greater pride, less shame, and a higher improvement-to-superiority goal ratio than social comparisons and no comparison; Comparing with a better past self elicited greater pride and lower shame than comparing with superior others. Future-self comparisons elicited greater pride, less shame, and a higher improvement-to-superiority goal ratio than social comparisons; Comparison with a worse future self preserved greater pride than comparison with superior others. Temporal comparisons, including both past-self and future-self comparisons, showed emotional and motivational advantages among Chinese children.

title: Do Large Language Models Walk Their Talk? Measuring the Gap Between Implicit Associations, Self-Report, and Behavioral Altruism
abstract: We investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit altruistic tendencies, and critically, whether their implicit associations and self-reports predict actual altruistic behavior. Using a multi-method approach inspired by human social psychology, we tested 24 frontier LLMs across three paradigms: (1) an Implicit Association Test (IAT) measuring implicit altruism bias, (2) a forced binary choice task measuring behavioral altruism, and (3) a self-assessment scale measuring explicit altruism beliefs. Our key findings are: (1) All models show strong implicit pro-altruism bias (mean IAT = 0.87, p < .0001), confirming models "know" altruism is good. (2) Models behave more altruistically than chance (65.6% vs. 50%, p < .0001), but with substantial variation (48-85%). (3) Implicit associations do not predict behavior (r = .22, p = .29). (4) Most critically, models systematically overestimate their own altruism, claiming 77.5% altruism while acting at 65.6% (p < .0001, Cohen's d = 1.08). This "virtue signaling gap" affects 75% of models tested. Based on these findings, we recommend the Calibration Gap (the discrepancy between self-reported and behavioral values) as a standardized alignment metric. Well-calibrated models are more predictable and behaviorally consistent; only 12.5% of models achieve the ideal combination of high prosocial behavior and accurate self-knowledge.

title: Assessment of child self-regulation: A review of ecological and structured approaches
abstract: The extent to which developmental science has mapped associations between cognitive, academic and socio-emotional functioning; caregiver reports and non-participant observation of young children was examined. Initially, 88 studies comprising over 300 effects were identified. The relationships between outcome measures and research design was described. Findings show that recurrent associations between task performance, behavioral report and naturalistic observation appear in this literature. The most frequently occurring comparisons in school settings were those between children’s disruptive-aggressive behavior, on-task/off-task behavior, prosocial behavior, externalizing problems, prosocial skills and early math and language achievement. In home settings, those between children’s positive/negative affect, engagement, compliance, temperament, cognitive and motor development were most common. Despite conceptual overlap, limited access to correlational data and between-study heterogeneity hinders cross-sample comparisons.

title: Role of Family Centered Care on Parental Stress and Anxiety Levels in Pediatric Intensive Care Unit.
abstract: To evaluate the impact of Family-Centered Care (FCC) practices on parental stress, anxiety, and depression among parents of children admitted to a Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU). This prospective observational study was conducted over one year (September 2024-August 2025) in a PICU of a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. Children aged 1 mo to 18 y admitted for more than 24 h were included. Parental psychological assessment was performed within 72 h of admission using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) and the Parental Stressor Scale (PSS). FCC components-including information sharing, family participation, presence during procedures and resuscitation, family-centered rounds, dignity and respect, negotiating roles, sharing goals, family conferences, and open visitation-were documented. Illness severity was assessed using PRISM scores. Correlation and comparative analyses were performed to examine associations between FCC practices and psychological outcomes. A total of 326 children were enrolled. Higher PRISM scores correlated strongly with increased parental stress (r = 0.793), anxiety (r = 0.721), and depression (r = 0.719) (p <0.0001). Implementation of key FCC components was significantly associated with lower stress, anxiety, and depression scores (p <0.05). The number of FCC components followed showed a strong inverse correlation with stress (r = -0.836), anxiety (r = -0.709), and depression (r = - 0.754) (p <0.0001). Open visitation alone was not significantly associated with improved psychological outcomes. Structured FCC practices are significantly associated with reduced parental stress, anxiety, and depression in the PICU. Strengthening meaningful family engagement may improve psychological outcomes in resource-limited critical care settings.

title: Network analysis of mental health literacy among adolescents and comparison of gender differences.
abstract: Mental health literacy serves as a crucial protective factor for adolescents when coping with psychological distress. To deeply investigate the structural characteristics of adolescents' mental health literacy, this study employed network analysis to construct the network structure of adolescents' mental health literacy, identify core nodes, and compare gender differences. A stratified random sampling method with grade as the classification variable was adopted to select 1,977 adolescents from grades 4 to 9 in Guangdong, China, to conduct the Adolescent Mental Health Literacy Scale survey. (1) The results of overall network estimation and inference showed that HS5 ("Talking improves mental health") in the help-seeking dimension had the highest expected influence index, followed by KMH1 ("Thoughts affect feelings") and KMI2 ("Mental disorders affect emotions"), indicating that these three nodes exerted the greatest influence on the item network. (2) The network comparison results demonstrated a significant difference between males and females in the invariance test of global strength (Male = 6.98, Female = 6.42; global strength difference = 0.56, p = 0.04). In the male network, the top three nodes in terms of expected influence index from high to low were HS3 ("Would disclose mental disorder"), HS1 ("Seek help if problems"), and HS4 ("Comfortable sharing with peers"). In the female network, the top three nodes in terms of expected influence index from high to low were HS5 ("Talking improves mental health"), KMI2 ("Mental disorders affect emotions"), and KMH1 ("Thoughts affect feelings"). The core node of adolescents' mental health literacy is HS5 ("Talking about my feelings with others helps promote mental health"). Further gender-specific analysis revealed that the core node of mental health literacy for male adolescents was HS3 ("I would actively seek help if I have psychological problems") in the help-seeking dimension, while for female adolescents, it was HS5 ("Talking about my feelings with others helps promote mental health") in the help-seeking dimension. Focusing on the help-seeking factor may be a significant intervention direction for enhancing adolescents' mental health literacy.

title: Moderate cardiac vagal tone predicts more cooperation in highly sensitive individuals
abstract: Cooperation, as a mutual collaboration, is a defining feature of human social life. Individual characteristics can influence cooperation. Recent studies have shown a quadratic relationship between cardiac vagal tone (CVT), an index of self-regulation, and prosocial behaviors. Individual differences in cooperation might also vary as a function of people's environmental sensitivity (ES), i.e., may be influenced by individual differences in the perception and processing of inner and external stimuli. We tested the direct and interactive effect of CVT and ES on cooperative behaviors in two independent samples. We measured heart rate and engagement in cooperative acts in 80 young adults (M = 23.61; SD = 1.60) who were also asked to self-report on ES. We found an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors. ES, on the other hand, did not predict differences in cooperative behaviors but moderated the relationships between CVT and cooperation, although the magnitude of this result was small. Specifically, only among individuals with higher ES cooperative behaviors change as a function of CVT. Highly sensitive individuals with lower or higher CVT, were less cooperative than low sensitive ones. Subsequently, we replicated the same study design in a second sample of 88 undergraduate students (M = 23.69; SD = 4.91). Once again, we found evidence supporting the presence of an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors, and we also found that ES moderated the relationships between the quadratic CVT term and cooperation.

title: Sessizliğin Psikolojisi: Gazze Soykırımı Özelinde Küresel Seyirci (Bystander) Davranışının Sosyal-Din Psikolojik Analizi
abstract: Kitlesel şiddet olaylarının yalnızca failler tarafından değil, aynı zamanda bu olaylar karşısında sessiz kalan ve eyleme geçmeyen geniş kitleler tarafından da sürdürüldüğü kabul edilmektedir. Sosyal psikoloji literatüründe bu durum seyirci (bystander) davranışı kavramı çerçevesinde ele alınmış ve çoğunlukla yüz yüze acil durumlar bağlamında incelenmiştir. Ancak günümüzde insani krizler giderek daha fazla dijital medya aracılığıyla deneyimlenmekte, bireyler şiddet ve acıya doğrudan değil, sosyal medya ve çevrim içi haber platformları üzerinden tanıklık etmektedir. Bu nedenle mevcut kuramsal yaklaşımlar, coğrafi olarak uzak ve dijital olarak dolayımlanmış kitlesel şiddet bağlamlarında ortaya çıkan eylemsizliği açıklamada yetersiz kalmaktadır. Bu çalışma, 7 Ekim 2023’ten itibaren Gazze’de devam eden kitlesel şiddet karşısında gözlenen küresel dijital seyirci davranışını açıklamaya yönelik kuramsal bir model önermektedir. Çalışmanın temel amacı, aynı dini kimliğe sahip olan bireylerden bir kısmı soykırıma uğrarken diğer bireylerin bu soykırıma neden seyirci davranışı olarak pasif kaldığını sosyal psikolojik olarak açıklamaktır. Din psikolojisi literatürü, dindarlığın empati, prososyal davranış ve ahlaki duyarlılıkla ilişkili olduğunu göstermesine rağmen, bu eğilimlerin her zaman eyleme dönüşmediği görülmektedir. Çalışma, bu paradoksu açıklamayı amaçlamaktadır. Makalede sosyal psikoloji, din psikolojisi ve kitlesel şiddet literatürü bütünleştirilerek beş katmanlı bir psikososyal model geliştirilmiştir. İlk katman olan yapısal katman, dijital uyaran fazlalığı, zaman baskısı ve bilişsel daralma süreçlerinin bireylerin ahlaki dikkatini sınırladığını ileri sürmektedir. İkinci katman olan bilişsel katman, sorumluluğun uluslararası kuruluşlar, devletler ve diğer güçlü aktörlere devredilmesini açıklamaktadır. Üçüncü katman olan sosyal-normatif katman, Sessizlik Sarmalı Kuramı ve çoğulcu cehalet kavramları aracılığıyla, bireylerin çevrelerindeki sessizliği toplumsal bir norm olarak algılamalarını ve bu nedenle görüşlerini ifade etmekten kaçınmalarını açıklamaktadır. Dördüncü katman olan ahlaki meşrulaştırma katmanı, adil dünya inancı, ahlaki çözülme ve insandışılaştırma mekanizmalarının eylemsizliği nasıl meşrulaştırdığını ortaya koymaktadır. Son katman olan duygusal katman ise merhamet yorgunluğu, duygusal küntleşme ve psişik uyuşma süreçlerinin bireylerin empatik tepkilerini nasıl zayıflattığını açıklamaktadır. Model, bu katmanların birbirinden bağımsız değil, geri-beslemeli bir döngü içerisinde işlediğini ileri sürmektedir. Yapısal baskılar bilişsel uzaklaşmayı, bilişsel süreçler normatif sessizliği, normatif sessizlik ahlaki meşrulaştırmayı, ahlaki meşrulaştırma ise duygusal tükenmeyi beslemektedir. Duygusal tükenme de bireyin dikkat ve duyarlılığını daha da azaltarak döngüyü yeniden üretmektedir. Çalışmanın din psikolojisine özgün katkısı, dinî kimliği yardım davranışını doğrudan belirleyen bir değişken olarak değil, tüm modelin işleyişini etkileyen bütünleşik bir moderatör olarak kavramsallaştırmasıdır. Dinî kimlik, belirli koşullar altında seyirci davranışını azaltabileceği gibi, bazı durumlarda bu davranışı derinleştirebilmektedir. Gazze bağlamında geliştirilen bu model, aynı zamanda dijital çağda ortaya çıkan diğer kitlesel şiddet ve soykırım örneklerinde gözlenen ahlaki eylemsizliği anlamak için de kullanılabilecek genel bir kuramsal çerçeve sunmaktadır.

title: Oxytocin restores context-specific hyperaltruistic preference
abstract: Recent advances in moral decision-making research show people are hyperaltruistic by being more willing to sacrifice monetary gains to spare others from suffering than to spare themselves. Yet other studies indicate an opposite egoistic bias: subjects are less willing to harm themselves for others' benefits than for their own. These results underscore the complexities of moral decisions and demand a mechanistic explanation for hyperaltruistic preferences. We investigated hyperaltruism using trade-off choices combining monetary gains and painful electric shocks and choices combining monetary losses and shocks. Study 1 revealed that switching the decision context from gains to losses effectively eliminated the hyperaltruistic preference, accompanied by the altered relationship between subjects' instrumental harm (IH) trait attitudes and relative pain sensitivities. In the pre-registered study 2, we found that oxytocin, a neuropeptide linked to parochial altruism, restored the context-dependent hyperaltruistic preference. Furthermore, oxytocin increased the degree to which subjects framed the task as harming others, which mediated the correlation between IH and relative pain sensitivities. Thus, the loss decision context and oxytocin diminished and restored the mediation effect of subjective harm framing, respectively. Our results help elucidate the psychological processes underpinning the contextual specificity of hyperaltruism and carry implications in promoting prosocial interactions.

title: Exploring Stakeholders' Perspectives on Required Nursing Competencies in Paediatric End-of-Life Care: A Qualitative Study.
abstract: To explore stakeholder perspectives (including nurses, nursing supervisors, educators and parents) on the competencies perceived as important for providing paediatric end-of-life care. A qualitative design using semi-structured interviews and a conventional content analysis approach was employed. Data were collected through individual, in-depth, semi-structured face-to-face interviews. Multi-stakeholder purposive sampling with maximum variation was utilized. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using conventional qualitative content analysis following Graneheim and Lundman's approach. Data collection and iterative analysis proceeded until code saturation was achieved within the healthcare professional cohort. Primary qualitative data were collected between 1 April and 30 June 2025, across paediatric healthcare settings in the North of Iran (Rasht, Guilan). Data sources comprised 17 participants: 15 healthcare professionals (10 clinical paediatric nurses, 2 nursing supervisors and 3 nursing faculty members) and 2 bereaved parents whose children had received end-of-life palliative care. Data analysis revealed one overarching theme, 'Providing comprehensive and ethically oriented care for the child and family at the end of life', encompassing six stakeholder-identified competencies (main categories) and 17 subcategories. The six proposed categories were: (1) competencies in ethical and empathetic communication; (2) competencies in comprehensive physical care focused on the child's quality of life; (3) competencies in psychological care and bereavement support; (4) competencies in cultural and spiritual care; (5) ethical and advanced clinical decision-making competencies; and (6) competencies in interdisciplinary and team-based collaboration. From the perspective of key stakeholders, competent paediatric end-of-life nursing care extends beyond routine clinical skills, requiring comprehensive, ethically grounded and context-sensitive capabilities for supporting both the dying child and their family. These preliminary, stakeholder-informed competencies highlight the need for strengthening specialized educational curricula and supportive institutional infrastructure to enhance the quality of paediatric end-of-life care. Culturally responsive care: Highlights the need to incorporate cultural and spiritual coping strategies-such as faith in divine providence-into paediatric palliative care competencies, extending beyond Western-oriented frameworks. Navigating ethical tensions: Equips nurses to effectively navigate complex ethical dilemmas and facilitate family-centred decision-making in healthcare settings characterized by limited resources and prominent religious frameworks. Educational framework: Offers an evidence-based foundation for developing specialized undergraduate curricula, continuous professional development programs and clinical protocols for general nurses providing end-of-life care. This study addresses the lack of context-specific evidence on paediatric end-of-life nursing competencies in Iran. The findings clarify the professional competencies required to support dignified, high-quality end-of-life care, preserve children's dignity and empower families during decision-making and bereavement. These results are anticipated to inform nurses, educators and healthcare policymakers involved in paediatric palliative care. This study was reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist. Bereaved parents whose children passed away in paediatric units participated as key interviewees, contributing directly to qualitative data generation by sharing their lived experiences and expectations regarding nursing competencies during their child's end-of-life trajectory.

title: Ethiopia's first health-sector public-private partnership: a qualitative evaluation of the design, procurement, and early implementation of an integrated diagnostic center.
abstract: Public-private partnerships (PPPs) are increasingly used to strengthen health systems in resource-constrained settings. In Ethiopia, PPPs in the health sector remain limited, with the Integrated Diagnostic Center (IDC) representing the first pilot initiative aimed at improving access to high-quality diagnostic services. This study aimed to evaluate the design, procurement, and contracting processes of the IDC PPP in Ethiopia and to generate lessons for future PPP development. A qualitative descriptive study was conducted using key informant interviews with nine stakeholders from government institutions, private sector partners, and implementing facilities. Participants were selected through purposive and snowball sampling techniques based on their knowledge and involvement in the program. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analyzed using thematic analysis with the support of Atlas.ti software. Five major themes emerged: (1) project design, procurement, and contracting; (2) financing and risk-sharing mechanisms; (3) service delivery and system readiness; (4) implementation challenges; and (5) recommendations and scalability. The IDC PPP follows a Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer (DBFOT) model, with predominantly private-sector financing complemented by public in-kind contributions. The project underwent extensive iterative processes across feasibility assessment, procurement, and contractual design, including adaptation of qualification criteria following an initial unsuccessful procurement round. Key challenges included regulatory gaps, limited institutional capacity, financial constraints, and external shocks such as COVID-19 and political instability. Risk mitigation mechanisms, including minimum revenue guarantees and revenue-sharing arrangements, were incorporated to address financial and operational uncertainties. Recommendations emphasized strengthening regulatory frameworks, enhancing institutional capacity, improving procurement alignment with market conditions, and integrating digital and operational systems. Scalability considerations further positioned the IDC as a model for potential expansion within the health system. The IDC PPP illustrates how health-sector PPPs can be developed in a resource-constrained setting through adaptive and iterative processes, despite significant regulatory, institutional, and financial constraints. The study highlights the importance of aligning procurement design with market capacity, strengthening institutional coordination, and embedding risk mitigation mechanisms in shaping PPP structures within evolving health systems.

title: Social Media, Self-Image, and Stigma in Cleft Lip and/or Palate: A Narrative Review.
abstract: ObjectiveCleft lip and/or palate (CL/P) are common congenital craniofacial anomalies associated with functional and psychosocial challenges. As social media platforms continue to expand, they increasingly influence perceptions of facial appearance, stigma, and social support among individuals with CL/P.DesignLiterature review and narrative synthesis of studies examine social media use and psychosocial experiences among individuals with CL/P and their families. A literature search was conducted across PubMed, Medline, Cochrane, Clarivate Web of Science, and ScienceDirect for studies published between January 2015 and October 2025. Studies examining social media use among individuals with CL/P, caregivers, or families were included. Eligible articles explored psychosocial experiences related to platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, Snapchat, and online support communities. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.Main Outcome MeasureThe impact of social media on self-awareness, stigma, and psychosocial experiences among individuals with CL/P and their families.ResultsAfter screening and eligibility assessment, 55 studies were included in the final synthesis. Social media was found to have both beneficial and detrimental effects. Appearance-focused platforms may contribute to social comparison, body image concerns, and experiences of stigma, particularly among adolescents. Online communities and support groups provide opportunities for peer support, information sharing, and advocacy, helping reduce isolation and improve coping among patients and families.ConclusionWhile certain platforms may exacerbate stigma and body image concerns, online support networks offer meaningful opportunities for connection, education, and empowerment.

title: Effects of Theory of Mind and Prosocial Beliefs on Steering Human-Aligned Behaviors of LLMs in Ultimatum Games
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in simulating human behaviors and performing theory-of-mind (ToM) reasoning, crucial for complex social interactions. We investigate ToM reasoning's role in aligning agentic behaviors with human norms in negotiation tasks, using the ultimatum game as our referenced task. We initialized LLM agents with different prosocial beliefs (Greedy, Fair, Selfless) and reasoning methods (chain of thought and ToM reasoning of varying levels), examining their decision-making processes and outcomes across multiple LLMs, including reasoning models like o3-mini and DeepSeek-R1 Distilled Qwen 32B. We perform 2,700 simulations to show that ToM reasoning enhances behavioral alignment with human norms, decision-making consistency, and negotiation outcomes. Consistent with prior findings, reasoning LLMs exhibit limited capability compared to ToM-enhanced LLMs, with different game roles benefiting from different ToM orders. Agents almost always chose strategies consistent with their assigned beliefs, and doing so aligned better with human norms in nearly every role, yet Greedy and Selfless agents still fell short of their norms in outcomes. Human verification further revealed that Llama 3.3 70B produces reasoning most consistent with its actions and beliefs. Our findings advance understanding of ToM's role in human-AI interaction and cooperative decision-making. The code used for our experiments can be found at https://github.com/Stealth-py/UltimatumToM.

title: Shifting the Smoking Cessation Landscape in Southeast Asia: Expert Perspectives and Recommendations.
abstract: Most Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) countries have ratified the World Health Organization Framework Convention on Tobacco Control and adopted MPOWER measures, but disparities persist regarding the help available to quit tobacco use, encompassing smoking cessation treatments, clinical practice guidelines, health care professional (HCP) training and policy implementation. This expert review evaluates the smoking cessation landscape across ASEAN, identifies barriers and proposes strategies to enhance cessation efforts. The ASEAN Advisory Board on Smoking Cessation, formed in 2023 with 9 experts from 7 countries, aimed to establish best practices and optimize pharmacological and behavioural interventions through a structured advisory board discussion. Two advisory board meetings in 2023 and 2024, supported by a targeted PubMed literature review, informed 12 recommendations to address gaps in pharmacotherapy access, behavioural support, HCP training and policy implementation. Key opportunities include standardized policies, advocating improved pharmacotherapy access, regulatory frameworks for each country and sharing HCP training resources and expertise. Areas of improvement for each country include integrating cessation services into primary care, expanding digital interventions and developing targeted strategies for high-risk populations, including pregnant women, adolescents and individuals with mental illnesses. Increased regional collaboration is vital for harmonizing policies, practices and HCP training, thus ensuring greater, more equitable access to evidence-based cessation support.

title: Rewriting the Divide: Child-Centred Participation and Theoretically Informed and Evidence-Based Intervention Design
abstract: Abstract This paper contributes to debates on problematic, dominant criminological narratives by foregrounding children’s own accounts of the support they need to thrive, informing ongoing efforts to support their individual and moral development. Drawing on community-based, participatory focus groups and individual and small-group interviews with 58 children aged 10–17 attending youth centres in Cambridge (UK), the study departs from deficit-oriented, adult-led explanations that frame children primarily through risk, mental disorders, or criminalisation. The findings rework prevailing criminological intervention approaches in two ways. First, using reflexive thematic analysis, the study centres children’s lived knowledge to identify trust, belonging, voice, agency, relational consistency of care, emotional support, and autonomy as central to what makes interventions trustworthy, accessible, engaging, and effective, whilst overly didactic, rigid, or authoritarian approaches were identified as key barriers to participation and effectiveness. These accounts move beyond adult assumptions about children’s needs, showing that effective support is grounded in relational, dialogic, autonomy-supportive environments rather than deficit-oriented models. Second, the paper argues that centring children’s perspectives is necessary but not sufficient: interventions must also be theoretically informed and evidence based. Rather than treating participatory and evidence-informed approaches as competing paradigms, the study offers data supporting their integration, combining child-centred qualitative insight with theoretically specified explanations of behaviour. Implications are discussed for the ongoing development of the school-based SATNAV:Compass youth intervention programme. This reconstruction of recommended intervention design approaches retains the strengths of existing traditions whilst addressing their limitations, offering a direction for future intervention research and practice.

title: Motor synchrony, social learning and closeness in group play settings.
abstract: Playful activities provide critical opportunities for rhythmic interactions, which may affect social and cognitive development in early childhood. Prior research suggests that motor synchrony promotes closeness and prosocial behaviour, but few studies have examined its role in social learning and in group settings. This study investigated whether motor synchrony in a clapping game, enhances preschoolers' closeness with others, imitation, over-imitation, and sharing behaviour. In a group setting, motor synchrony and asynchrony were experimentally induced between the child and two experimenters. We hypothesized that children would feel closer, imitate more, and share more with an adult partner who moved in synchrony compared to one who moved asynchronously. Bayesian analyses revealed no credible evidence that the children affiliated, imitated, over-imitated, or shared differently with their synchronous vs. asynchronous partner (BF10 = 0.045-0.216). Manipulation checks indicated that although the adults adhered to the stimuli, there was overall low motor synchrony. These findings highlight the challenges of inducing motor synchrony in playful group settings and raise questions about the level of synchrony necessary to impact social affiliation and learning in young children.

title: Emergence of Fairness Behavior Driven by Reputation-Based Voluntary Participation in Evolutionary Dictator Games
abstract: Recently, reputation-based indirect reciprocity has been widely applied to the study on fairness behavior. Previous works mainly investigate indirect reciprocity by considering compulsory participation. While in reality, individuals may choose voluntary participation according to the opponent's reputation. It is still unclear how such reputation-based voluntary participation influences the evolution of fairness. To address this question, we introduce indirect reciprocity with voluntary participation into the dictator game (DG). We respectively consider good dictators or recipients can voluntarily participate in games when the opponents are assessed as bad. We theoretically calculate the fairness level under all social norms of third-order information. Our findings reveal that several social norms induce the high fairness level in both scenarios. However, more social norms lead to a high fairness level for voluntary participation of recipients, compared with the one of good dictators. The results also hold when the probability of voluntary participation is not low. Our results demonstrate that recipients’ voluntary participation is more effective in promoting the emergence of fairness behavior.

title: Attitudes toward using non-medical eligibility criteria for publicly funded IVF: a population survey in Belgium.
abstract: Assisted Reproductive Technologies (ART) such as in-vitro fertilization (IVF) are often reimbursed based on non-medical eligibility criteria, such as patients' age, marital status, relationship type or reproductive history. These criteria reflect normative assumptions about parenthood and remain ethically contested. This study investigates the Belgian public's awareness of and attitudes toward the use of such non-medical criteria in reimbursing IVF and identifies socio-demographic patterns underlying these views. A sample of 3,000 adults (18-70y) completed an online survey that elicited attitudes towards public funding of IVF and using funding restrictions based on patients' age, partner age and gender, relationship type, number of prior children, and different infertility etiologies. Latent class cluster analysis (LCCA) was used to detect opinion subgroups, and logistic regression to assess socio-demographic predictors of subgroup membership. Although there was strong overall support for public reimbursement of IVF, respondents showed limited knowledge about eligibility criteria within the Belgian system. Majorities endorsed several eligibility restrictions, including those based on maternal age (74%), partner age (57%), number of prior biological children (60%), and consciously delayed childbearing (70%). Two thirds opposed prioritizing heterosexual couples. LCCA revealed three distinct opinion profiles (generous, moderately restrictive, and highly restrictive), primarily differentiated by the perceived generosity of current Belgian policy, access for same-sex couples and single mothers, and the acceptability of patient copayments. Parenthood experience and prior infertility were significant predictors of profile membership. This study finds widespread public support for reimbursing fertility treatment within Belgian healthcare, but also for using eligibility criteria that extend beyond the currently used, sole criterion of maternal age. In the light of growing infertility rates, pressured ART budgets and the limited awareness of the current policy observed in this survey, these results underscore the need for further societal debate on priority setting in Belgian infertility care.

title: Effects of Classroom Intervention on Problematic Behavior of Grade 2 Pupils in Lian Central School
abstract: This study investigated the effects of classroom interventions on the problematic behavior of Grade 2 pupils at Lian Central School. It specifically examined the pupils’ profile in terms of age, gender, socioeconomic background, family structure, and academic performance; identified common problematic behaviors such as inattentiveness, disruptive classroom conduct, aggression or oppositional behavior, lack of participation, and peer-related conflicts; and determined the classroom interventions implemented to address these concerns. The study employed a descriptive-quantitative research design and involved Grade 2 pupils and their teachers. Data were gathered through a researcher-made questionnaire and analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and correlation analysis. The findings showed that teachers employed a variety of classroom interventions, particularly positive reinforcement and socio-emotional strategies. Giving praise or verbal recognition was the most frequently reported positive reinforcement strategy, with 85.0% of responses, followed by the use of stars, stickers, or points at 77.5%. Among socio-emotional interventions, morning meetings or sharing circles were most frequently implemented at 62.5%, followed by role-playing activities for empathy and respect at 60.0%. These findings indicate that behavioral management at Lian Central School involves multiple approaches that emphasize positive reinforcement, emotional development, participation, and constructive peer relationships rather than relying solely on punitive discipline. The study further revealed that pupil characteristics were associated with selected dimensions of problematic behavior. Academic performance and socioeconomic background emerged as important factors, while age, gender, and parents’ occupation showed significant relationships, particularly with aggression. Family structure was significantly associated with disruptive conduct and showed a borderline relationship with participation. The findings also identified implementation challenges, particularly insufficient parental support, pupils’ tendency to forget behavioral rules, large class sizes, difficulty maintaining consistent discipline, and peer influence. Overall, the study highlights the importance of sustained, developmentally appropriate, and context-sensitive classroom interventions supported by strong teacher–pupil relationships and home–school collaboration.

title: Beauty growth-mindset promotes prosocial and altruistic behavior
abstract: The effects of beauty on judgment and behavior are well-established and somewhat "unidirectional" (i.e., it seems that only beautiful people reap social benefits). In particular, a person's beauty does not seem to have any effect on his/her own prosocial behavior. In the current research, we focus on how people relate themselves to beauty, namely beauty mindset, and how it may shape prosocial and altruistic behavior. We present 10 experiments (N = 4,449). Participants who hold a beauty growth-mindset (i.e., believing that beauty is improvable) donated more money to charity (vs. fixed-mindset), were more likely to get vaccinated against COVID-19 after exposure to an intervention focusing on herd-protection (vs. self-protection), and showed increased intention to engage in other forms of prosocial and altruistic behavior. Empirically, these effects are mediated by a self-perception of the ability to exert impact on others. The present research serves as a starting point for investigating how beauty growth-mindset brings profound societal effects such as promoting prosociality.

title: Temporal changes in immunization information systems across U.S. states and jurisdictions, 2000-2024.
abstract: Statewide immunization data are essential for monitoring vaccination trends and evaluating immunization program impact. In the United States, Immunization Information Systems (IIS) were established in the early 1990s to collect these data; however, operational, legal, and procedural details vary across states and over time. This study summarized differences in IIS characteristics, such as legal requirements and reporting procedures, across U.S. states and jurisdictions over time. We compiled jurisdiction-level IIS regulatory data from published studies and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) surveys conducted in 2000, 2012, 2018, and 2024 to compare changes in age-group coverage, provider reporting requirements, consent procedures, operating authority, and data-sharing regulations. Between 2000 and 2024, legal frameworks and reporting practices for immunization registries expanded across U.S. states and jurisdictions. The number of states with laws or administrative rules authorizing immunization registries increased from 24 states in 2000 to all 50 states, Washington, D·C., five metropolitan areas, five U.S. territories, and three Freely Associated States in 2024. Over the same period, reporting requirements also became more widespread. The number of states and jurisdictions mandating providers to report immunization records increased from 12 (24% of 51) in 2000 to 54 (84% of 64) in 2024. Consent policies also changed over time. By 2024, most states and jurisdictions had adopted implicit consent for reporting children's immunization records (41/64; 64%), while a smaller proportion required explicit parental consent (7/64, 11%) or implemented mandatory participation without consent (14/64, 22%). IIS infrastructure and reporting requirements have expanded across U.S. states and jurisdictions over the past two decades, while heterogeneity in consent policies and reporting practices persists. These temporal changes may need to be considered when interpreting IIS data, particularly in longitudinal and cross-jurisdictional analyses.

title: Malaria and associated factors after RTS,S/AS01 vaccination in children in Komenda-Edina-Eguafo-Abrem Municipality, Ghana: A facility-based cross-sectional study.
abstract: ObjectiveMalaria remains a major public health challenge in Ghana despite the implementation of multiple control measures, including the RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) malaria vaccine. This study assessed malaria rapid diagnostic test positivity and associated factors among individuals presenting with suspected malaria in the Komenda-Edina-Eguafo-Abrem District, Ghana.MethodsThis facility-based cross-sectional study included 400 individuals of all age groups who presented with suspected malaria at the Salvation Army Hospital, Ajumako Ba. Malaria was diagnosed using rapid diagnostic tests. Data on sociodemographic characteristics, malaria control practices, environmental exposures, and vaccination status were collected using structured questionnaires. Associations were assessed using chi-square tests and binary logistic regression to identify independent predictors of malaria infection.ResultsThe overall malaria rapid diagnostic test positivity rate was 20.8% (83/400). Malaria test positivity differed significantly by age (p < 0.001), with the highest burden observed among children and adolescents. Sleeping under a mosquito net the preceding night was strongly protective (adjusted odds ratio = 0.17, 95% confidence interval: 0.07-0.40, p < 0.001). In contrast, sharing mosquito nets with one person (adjusted odds ratio = 4.51, 95% confidence interval: 1.31-15.50, p = 0.02), with more than one person (adjusted odds ratio = 4.76, 95% confidence interval: 0.92-24.47, p = 0.06), prolonged nocturnal outdoor activity (adjusted odds ratio = 4.49, 95% confidence interval: 1.44-14.03, p = 0.01), and proximity to gullies or stagnant water (adjusted odds ratio = 2.49, 95% confidence interval: 1.24-5.01, p = 0.01) significantly increased malaria risk. Among children younger than 7 years, malaria prevalence was lower in RTS,S/AS01-vaccinated children (29.6%) compared to unvaccinated children (60%), although differences were not statistically significant overall. Significant associations in this age group were observed with mosquito net use, nocturnal outdoor activity, and nearby vegetation.ConclusionMalaria rapid diagnostic test positivity remains high in the Komenda-Edina-Eguafo-Abrem Municipality, particularly among children. Mosquito net use, nocturnal outdoor activity, and proximity to potential mosquito breeding sites were associated with rapid diagnostic test positivity. The small vaccine-eligible subgroup limited conclusions on RTS,S/AS01 vaccination. Integrated, community-based malaria control strategies remain essential for sustained reductions in malaria transmission.

title: B-cell receptor repertoire remodeling in Kawasaki disease is associated with clonal expansion and distinct repertoire features in coronary artery lesions.
abstract: Kawasaki disease (KD) is an acute systemic vasculitis in children, but the characteristics of the B-cell receptor (BCR) repertoire during acute disease and their association with coronary artery lesions (CALs) remain poorly understood. High-throughput sequencing of BCR heavy-chain (BCR-H) CDR3 regions was performed in 22 children, including 9 healthy controls and 13 patients with KD, of whom 9 had no CAL and 4 had CAL. Repertoire diversity, clonal expansion, immunoglobulin isotype distribution, V-J gene usage, CDR3 characteristics, and inter-individual and cross-isotype repertoire sharing were systematically evaluated. KD exhibited reduced BCR repertoire diversity, with a significant decrease in IgM diversity. The repertoire showed increased contributions of high-frequency and hyperexpanded clonotypes, with the most pronounced expansion in patients with CAL. IgM displayed the strongest clonal remodeling, characterized by reduced low-frequency and increased highly abundant clonotypes. KD also showed selective alterations in IGHV usage and V-J gene pairing. CAL was associated with increased IGHA usage and changes in CDR3 amino acid composition. Substantial inter-individual CDR3 sharing was observed among KD patients, and 20 recurrent clonotypes absent from healthy controls were identified as candidate KD-associated sequences. Cross-isotype CDR3 sharing also tended to be higher in KD, particularly among patients with CAL. Acute KD is characterized by substantial BCR repertoire remodeling, marked by selective IgM clonal expansion, repertoire convergence, and CAL-associated IgA-biased remodeling. These findings provide new insights into humoral immune dysregulation in KD and identify candidate B-cell clonotypes for further investigation of disease pathogenesis and coronary involvement.

title: Conjoined Twin Separation and Reconstruction: An Anatomical Classification System, Techniques, and Outcomes at a Tertiary Pediatric Care Center.
abstract: Conjoined twin separation is highly complex. Existing taxonomies describe morphology but not the extent of sharing across regions-a key determinant of feasibility, planning, and outcomes. The authors introduce the Texas Children's Hospital classification system and report their institutional experience, supplemented by a structured literature review. The authors conducted a retrospective review of conjoined twins (2014 to 2024). The Texas Children's Hospital system assigns 1 point per domain (eg, skin/soft tissue, deep viscera, major vascular, central neurological, and bone) within 4 regions (eg, cranium, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis); region scores yield a composite fusion score. Two reviewers scored cases. The authors described outcomes and compared composite fusion scores between separated and nonseparated twins. A PubMed review identified cases with anatomical detail for scoring. Seventeen cases were identified; 12 of 17 (70.6%) were viable at birth, and 4 of 12 (33.3%; 4 of 17, 23.5% overall) underwent elective separation. Tissue expansion preceded separation in 3 of 4 pairs (75%); hepatic artery embolization was performed in 1 of 4 (25%). Device complications occurred in 2 of 3 tissue expansion pairs; sternal hardware complications occurred in 2 of 3 plated patients. Infection and seroma each occurred in 2 of 8 patients (25%). Three of 8 patients (37.5%) required tracheostomy and 3 (37.5%), gastrostomy. All separated twins survived (follow-up 9 to 117 months). Composite fusion score was lower in separated versus nonseparated twins in both institutional (mean [SD], 5.2 [2.8] versus 9.3 [3.2]; P = 0.041) and literature cohorts (4.7 [1.9] versus 7.1 [1.8]; P = 0.010). The Texas Children's Hospital classification offers an adjunctive, anatomy-based framework capturing the burden of shared structures and is associated with separation feasibility. Although not predictive, it provides a common language to align teams, structure operative strategy, and support counseling.

title: School-Age Differences in Reasonable Accommodations for Students Who Stutter: A Content Analysis of Medical Letters.
abstract: Japanese schools must provide reasonable accommodations for students who stutter, but developmental variations in these needs are poorly understood. This study characterized accommodation requests in clinician-drafted medical letters to clarify these needs. Medical letters for 116 students who stutter (65 elementary, 51 secondary) were retrospectively analyzed. Accommodation content was classified using inductive content analysis. Group proportions were compared, and stuttering frequency (%SS) and social anxiety (LSAS-CA) were analyzed descriptively. Five accommodation categories were identified. Elementary students significantly more frequently requested teacher-mediated protective support, such as reporting teasing and classroom stuttering explanations. Secondary students more frequently requested social functioning accommodations, including subject-teacher information sharing and entrance examination support. Presentation-related accommodations were highly prevalent across both groups (61.2% overall). Participants who completed the anxiety assessment exhibited elevated social anxiety (mean LSAS-CA: 42.1). Accommodation needs reflect structural school transitions, shifting from classroom protection under the elementary homeroom system to social participation support under the secondary subject-teacher system. Importantly, presentation-related needs represent a consistent concern, likely driven by subjective anxiety rather than objective stuttering severity. Medical letters may serve as valuable tools for initiating constructive clinician-family-school dialogue to facilitate tailored support.

title: Empathy as a crucial skill in disrupting disparities in global brain health.
abstract: Brain health refers to the state of a person's brain function across various domains, including cognitive, behavioral and motor functions. Healthy brains are associated with better individual health, increased creativity, and enhanced productivity. A person's brain health is intricately connected to personal, social and environmental factors. Racial, ethnic, and social disparities affect brain health and on the global scale these disparities within and between regions present a hurdle to brain health. To overcome global disparities, greater collaboration between practitioners and healthcare providers and the people they serve is essential. This requires cultural humility driven by empathy. Empathy is a core prosocial value, a cognitive-emotional skill that helps us understand ourselves and others. This position paper aims to provide an overview of the vital roles of empathy, cooperation, and interdisciplinary partnerships. By consciously integrating this understanding in practice, leaders can better position themselves to address the diverse challenges faced by communities, promote inclusivity in policies and practices, and further more equitable solutions to the problem of global brain health.

title: The Good Samaritan Myth: Why Virtue-based Food Waste Policy Fails and What Should Replace It
abstract: For nearly fifty years, federal corporate food waste legislation has consistently employed an aretaic (virtue-based) theoretical framework that assumes corporations will act as “Good Samaritans” when provided with appropriate incentives and liability protections. Beginning with Federal Tax Code Section 170(e)(3) in 1976 and continuing through the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act (1996), the Federal Food Donation Act (2008), the Agri-cultural Improvement Act (2018), and the Food Donation Improvement Act (2022), United States policy has relied exclusively on voluntary compliance mechanisms rather than mandatory regulations. This Article argues that this approach is built on a myth, and that the myth operates on three interlocking levels. At the legislative level, it holds that corporations will donate surplus food if liability barriers are removed, a claim that fifty years of evidence has consistently refuted. At the hermeneutic level, it misreads the parable of the Good Samaritan itself: corporations in the food waste context are not the Samaritan, who acted voluntarily out of genuine compassion, but the innkeeper, who provided services in exchange for guaranteed payment. At the ideological level, it assumes that virtue can be cultivated in profit-driven entities whose fiduciary obligations run not to hungry communities but to shareholders. The consequences of this myth are measurable. Despite decades of tax incentives and liability shields, corporate food waste has increased from 30% of the available food supply in 1974 to nearly 40% today, while 47.4 million Americans experience food insecurity. Food waste in United States landfills generates 34% of all human-related methane emissions, substantially con-tributing to climate change that disproportionately harms the communities that food donation policies were designed to serve. The persistence of incidents like the 2021 Portland Fred Meyer controversy—where thousands of pounds of edible food were discarded and guarded from recovery by residents during a community crisis—demonstrates that voluntary approaches fail precisely when they are needed most. Even industry leaders fall short: after nine years of its Zero Hunger | Zero Waste initiative, Kroger, ranked first among United States supermarket chains for food waste commitment by the Center for Biological Diversity in 2019, only achieved a cumulative food waste reduction of less than 4% against a stated goal of 50% by 2025. This Article provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of United States corporate food waste legislation, examining why virtue-based approaches have systematically failed to address the interconnected crises of food waste, food insecurity, and environmental harm. The analysis demonstrates that aretaic theory, which seeks to cultivate virtue through indirect encouragement rather than direct mandates, is fundamentally incompatible with corporate shareholder theory and profit-maximization imperatives. The Article further critiques France’s Garot Law, which mandates supermarket food donations through categorical duties, demonstrating that while this deontological approach achieved impressive increases in food donations, it failed to meaningfully reduce overall food insecurity due to its rigid, context-insensitive framework and the absence of monitoring capacity sufficient to ensure that donated food reached food-insecure communities. Moving beyond these existing approaches, this Article proposes a consequentialist-based Corporate Partner Food Waste Act, grounded in Congress’ Commerce Clause authority and administered by the EPA. Rather than assuming corporations will choose to do good, the Act would ensure they do good as a natural consequence of pursuing their interests within a well-designed system of mandatory requirements and measurable outcomes. The framework establishes food recovery requirements differentiated by geographic proximity to food-insecure communities—using USDA Food Access Research Atlas definitions as the baseline—creating “Priority Zones” and “Standard Zones” with distinct obligations tied to community need. Penalties are anchored to company revenue rather than fixed amounts, ensuring that the cost of non-compliance consistently exceeds the cost of compliance regardless of a company’s size. Annual performance reviews, comprehensive data collection, and an EPA Food Waste Reduction Coordinator provide the monitoring infrastructure that voluntary frameworks have consistently lacked. After five decades of legislative failure, this Article argues that the path forward requires abandoning the Good Samaritan myth entirely and replacing it with a regulatory framework that treats corporations not as potential virtuous actors, but as corporate partners whose obligations are enforceable, measurable, and calibrated to actual outcomes.
