title: Cost-benefits analysis of joint actions; children and adults estimate the potential effort of acting together.
abstract: Every day we engage in activities that require collaboration and assistance from others. Social interactions with children are distinct because they frequently result in partners contributing different amounts of effort. This study investigates the decision-making processes underpinning joint actions; specifically, whether children and adults estimate they will have to invest different amounts of effort when engaging in joint tasks compared to doing the same task by themselves. In 4 Experiments, children and adults estimated the weight of objects when they anticipated that they would be lifted alone and when they thought they would have help. Children and adults estimated the weight of 3 clear baskets carrying different weights (light, medium, and heavy). The estimated weight of objects varied for adults and children depending on whether they thought they would lift alone or together. Children reliably perceived objects as lighter when they expected help from their parent compared to lifting them alone or with the help of a sibling. Parents, in turn, estimated objects would be heavier when they were helping their child. Overall, results suggest that we analyze the costs and benefits of helping another person and the social bond we have with them before engaging in joint actions.

title: Why are younger-age adults reluctant to give blood? A reflexive thematic analysis of non-donors in the United Kingdom
abstract: The present study explored the psychosocial factors influencing blood donation behaviour among younger-age adults classified as non-donors in the United Kingdom. Six participants (aged 18–35) with no history of blood donation were recruited via opportunity sampling. Semi-structured interviews were conducted and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify key patterns in participant narratives related to donation behaviour. Two overarching themes were identified. Barriers to blood donation included four sub-themes: (i) socially constructed misconceptions of eligibility and need, (ii) embodied discomfort and perceived invasiveness of the donation process, (iii) disengagement and deferred responsibility in blood donation, and (iv) perceived absence and inaccessibility of blood donation campaigns. Facilitators of blood donation included three sub-themes: (i) promoting blood donation by addressing diverse reward preferences, (ii) the importance of procedural clarity in reducing uncertainty, and (iii) increasing motivation to donate blood through cues to act. Tailored public health strategies must address adult non-donors’ psychological and informational barriers, including misconceptions, procedural uncertainty, and anxiety about physical reactions. Interventions should pair targeted communication with accessible, accurate information and frame donation as both socially beneficial and personally rewarding.

title: Early social-cognitive development as a dynamic developmental system—a lifeworld approach
abstract: Based on developmental systems and dynamic systems theories, we propose the lifeworld approach-a conceptual framework for research and a hypothesis concerning early social-cognitive development. As a framework, the lifeworld approach recognizes the social embeddedness of development and shifts the focus away from individual developmental outcomes toward the reciprocal interplay of processes within and between individuals that co-constitutes early social-cognitive development. As a hypothesis, the lifeworld approach proposes that the changing developmental system-spanning the different individuals as their subsystems-strives toward attractor states through regulation at the behavioral level, which results in both the emergence and further differentiation of developmental attainments. The lifeworld approach-as a framework and a hypothesis, including key methodological approaches to test it-is exemplified by research on infants' self-awareness, prosocial behavior and social learning. Equipped with, first, a conceptual framework grounded in a modern view on development and, second, a growing suite of methodological approaches, developmental science can advance by analyzing the mutually influential relations between intra-individual and interactional processes in order to identify key mechanisms underlying early social-cognitive development.

title: Prognostic value of modified thrombelastometry for thromboembolic risk stratification in neurosurgical patients: protocol for a prospective, multicenter, observational study (TENS).
abstract: Neurosurgical patients, particularly those with intracranial tumours such as glioma or meningioma, face a markedly elevated risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), with reported rates of deep vein thrombosis between 15% and 70% depending on tumour entity and surgical extent. Current prophylactic strategies rely predominantly on pharmacological and mechanical measures and do not account for the individual complexity of coagulation dynamics. Modified thromboelastometry, employing a low-dose tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) test, enables functional assessment of both fibrinolytic capacity and prothrombotic states at the point of care. We hypothesize that preoperative and perioperative thromboelastometric parameters - in particular lysis time (LT) in the low-dose TPA test - are associated with the occurrence of thromboembolic events in neurosurgical patients. TENS is a prospective, multicenter, observational prognostic factor study targeting 350 evaluable participants (up to 369 enrolled to account for attrition) across four university hospitals in Cologne, Munich (two centres), and Oldenburg. Eligible patients are adults (≥ 18 years) scheduled for neurosurgical procedures involving intracranial tumour resection or with an anticipated operative duration of ≥ 4 h. Thromboelastometric measurements (EXTEM, INTEM, FIBTEM, low-dose TPA test) are performed at three defined time points: before surgery, at the end of surgery, and on postoperative day 1. The primary objective is to assess the prognostic association between lysis time (LT) in the low-dose TPA test and objectively imaging-confirmed venous thromboembolic events occurring within 30 days after surgery. Secondary endpoints comprise further thromboelastometric parameters, standard coagulation laboratory values, and clinical outcomes including length of hospital stay, duration of surgery, ICU stay, and days at home at day 30. Modified thromboelastometry has the potential to improve individualised risk stratification for thromboembolism in neurosurgical patients. If lysis time in the low-dose TPA test demonstrates prognostic value for thromboembolic events, this could inform the development of novel diagnostic and therapeutic algorithms for high-risk surgical populations. Deutsches Register Klinischer Studien (DRKS), No. DRKS00034388, registered October 8, 2024. Anonymised participant-level data and the statistical analysis code will be made available upon reasonable request to the corresponding author following publication of the primary results, subject to applicable data protection regulations and the terms of the institutional data sharing agreement (see chapter The full study protocol will be publicly accessible via the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS, No. DRKS00034388). The study is currently in active recruitment. Recruitment was initiated at the coordinating centre in Cologne on 19 December 2024, with additional centres opening after completion of their local approval and site-initiation processes. As of March 2026, fewer than 50% of the target sample of 350 evaluable participants had been enrolled. Recruitment is expected to be completed by March 2027.

title: Encouraging Ethical and Practical Local Government Managers: How the ICMA Code of Ethics Promotes Servant Leadership
abstract: This study empirically examined the association between the adoption of ethical codes and servant leadership in local government organizations. Analyzing survey data from the International City/County Management Association (ICMA) from 2012-2018, along with the U.S. Census Bureau’s Community Engagement and Volunteering Supplement (CEVS) to the 2021 Current Population Survey (CPS), this study explored how the associations between adoption, scope, and enforcement mechanism of ethical codes impacted seven categories of servant leadership: relationships with elected officials, policy collaboration, information exchange, innovation, performance effectiveness, service delivery, and public/community engagement. This study also explored the relationship between ethics training and these seven dimensions of servant leadership. Although evidence suggests that compliance-based ethics infrastructure such as ethical code adoption and a broadly-applying ethical code scope is associated with servant leadership, integrity-based ethics initiatives, namely a robust, continuous ethics training program, shows the strongest association with servant leadership outcomes in local government.

title: What is associated with openness to integrated sport among school-aged youth with disabilities? A cross-sectional study from Hungary.
abstract: Integrated sport-defined here as people with and without disabilities sharing a sport setting-may support social connection and opportunities for participation, but integration does not by itself establish inclusion, and stated openness is not actual participation. This cross-sectional study examined factors associated with whether school-aged youth with disabilities in Hungary said they would like to take part in an integrated sports club. A survey of 1,298 youth with disabilities aged 8-18 was conducted with the support of a national disability-sport federation. The single-item outcome retained its three nominal response options-"yes," "no," and "not interested"-without assuming that the latter two captured active refusal and passive disengagement. Gaussian latent profile analysis summarised seven activity-limitation indicators; a categorical latent class model tested sensitivity to their ordinal measurement; and multinomial logistic regression assessed associations with limitation severity, impairment type, awareness, access, attitude, and school type. Activity limitation formed a low-to-high severity gradient. Average posterior classification probabilities were .953, .902, and .938, and the categorical sensitivity model reproduced the ordered structure (87.6% identical ordered assignment; adjusted Rand index = .689). The full multinomial model had modest explanatory power (McFadden's The findings identify correlates of a stated, unvalidated openness item, not causes of inclusion or participation. Their interpretation is limited by the cross-sectional convenience sample, single-item measures, modest model fit, and the absence of participant-level records of questionnaire mode or pictorial support.

title: Measuring dispositional empathy in South African children.
abstract: Empathy is a key factor to examine in development, because of its predictive associations with both aggression and successful prosocial behaviour. However, established measures of empathy for Low-to-Middle Income Countries, including South Africa, are lacking. In children, parent-report measures are key. However, a local study examining empathy and aggression (Malcolm-Smith We contrasted internal consistency reliability of a simplified version of the GEM (SGEM; The parent-report version of the QCAE performed well as a measure of child dispositional cognitive and affective empathy, with good reliability (overall α = 0.90 vs. SGEM α = .63), and confirmatory factor analysis supporting the two-factor structure. The SGEM's reliability and failure to correlate with QCAE indicated poor psychometric performance. This is the first psychometric evaluation of the QCAE as a parent-report measure, and our results indicate that it should prove useful for future assessments of dispositional empathy in children across a variety of contexts.

title: The Evolved Nest in Childhood: Relation to Adult Well-being and Social Capital Across Cultures
abstract: Abstract Evolved nests are species-specific developmental systems that support biological, psychological, and social needs. The human evolved nest includes practices such as responsive care, self-directed play, and extensive affectionate touch. Previous studies have linked childhood experience of these practices to both child and adult well-being. Here we assessed whether recall of evolved nest experiences during childhood (age 0–18) was related to three dimensions of adult well-being and social capital (personal well-being, social relationships, and general prosociality) in three countries (USA, UK, Japan). Recalled evolved nest experience was positively associated with multiple measures under each dimension across cultures after controlling for demographic factors ( n = 1,401). In contrast, it was not found to be associated with incentivised measures of prosociality (elicited via a series of economic games) in any country. Exploratory factor analyses revealed that experiences of evolved nest practices clustered together under two common factors in each country: positive and negative experiences. These factors were independently associated with multiple indicators of adult well-being and social capital in each country, and these associations were generally stronger for positive (vs. negative) experiences. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that childhood experience of the evolved nest has long-term benefits for individual and societal well-being regardless of cultural differences.

title: Depth or Breadth? The Impacts of Monetary Incentives on the Direction of Free Knowledge Contributions
abstract: In this study, we examine how changes in monetary incentives offered to online consultants on e-consultation platforms shape the direction of their free knowledge contributions across specialized and non-specialized domains. We use the sudden suspension and subsequent resumption of the Fenda platform as two exogenous shocks to the monetary incentives these online consultants receive, and implement a difference-in-differences estimation. Our study shows that monetary incentives shift the direction of online consultants’ free knowledge contributions. Rather than delving deeper into their specialized domains and engaging with even unpopular topics, they tend to broaden their contributions across a broader array of non-specialized domains. The findings enrich the literature on knowledge management and provide valuable guidance for managers of e-consultation platforms.

title: Timmy’s Trip to Planet Earth: The Long-Term Effects of a Social and Emotional Education Program for Preschool Children
abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Social and Emotional Education (SEE) interventions during early childhood have shown considerable promise in enhancing children's emotion understanding, social competence, and behavioural adjustments. However, few studies have examined their long-term impact, especially across the preschool-to-primary school transition. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a manualized SEE program, Timmy's Trip to Planet Earth, in promoting emotional, behavioural, and social functioning over time. METHODS: = 44). The program combined teacher training, classroom-based lessons, home activities, and teachers' ongoing implementation support. The effectiveness of the program was measured via the Test of Emotion Comprehension (TEC), the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), and the Social Competence and Behavior Evaluation (SCBE-30). RESULTS: Significant Time × Group interactions were observed for the TEC External and Mental components, indicating greater improvements in emotion recognition and mental state understanding in the intervention group. The SDQ revealed significant reductions in conduct problems and increased prosocial behaviours. In the SCBE-30, a significant interaction effect was found for social competence, with the intervention group showing greater improvement over time compared to the control group. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that SEE programs can produce meaningful and lasting improvements in children's emotional and social skills across key educational transitions. Teacher training and family involvement likely played a critical role in supporting the program's sustained impact.

title: Sensitivity and Criterion Validity of ED100K Lifetime Eating Disorder Diagnoses: A Study Using a National Eating Disorder Quality Register.
abstract: Epidemiological and genomic studies of eating disorders (ED) require scalable approaches to case ascertainment. The self-report ED100K questionnaire assesses lifetime ED diagnoses, has been translated into several languages, and has been used in large cohort studies, with data shared or planned for sharing through major repositories and the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium. This retrospective diagnostic validation study linked ED100K data from the Eating Disorders Genetics Initiative-Sweden (EDGI-SE), a case-control cohort, with clinician-assigned diagnoses from the Swedish national quality register for EDs (Riksät). In the subset with Riksät-linked specialist care records (n = 6889), the sensitivity of ED100K-derived lifetime DSM-IV diagnoses, DSM-5 anorexia nervosa (AN), and broadly defined binge-eating behavior (BE-BROAD) was evaluated against clinician-interview diagnoses. In the full EDGI-SE cohort (N = 15,699), comprising community-ascertained cases and controls, criterion validity was assessed via associations with ED specialist care. Sensitivity was high for AN (DSM-IV: 0.84, DSM-5: 0.96) and substantially lower for bulimia nervosa (BN; 0.61) and binge-eating disorder (BED; 0.34). Sensitivity for BE-BROAD was high (0.88), exceeding BN and BED. Most individuals with BN or BED in specialist care not identified with corresponding ED100K diagnoses were captured by broader ED100K classifications, including BE-BROAD and DSM-5 diagnoses. All ED100K diagnoses and BE-BROAD were strongly associated with ED specialist care, providing evidence for the criterion validity of ED100K ED diagnoses. The ED100K shows strong sensitivity for lifetime AN and BE-BROAD. Lower sensitivity for BN and BED likely reflects challenges in retrospective self-report (e.g., recalling frequency and duration) and in capturing diagnostic features requiring greater subjective judgment. Broader binge-eating classifications may better capture cases missed by algorithm-based BN and BED diagnoses. EDGI is a registered clinical trial (clinicaltrials.gov ID: NCT04378101).

title: Effective altruism, technoscience and the making of philanthropic value
abstract: A recent philanthropic movement with advocates among high-profile tech entrepreneurs and philosophers, effective altruism (EA) has been widely disparaged for its flawed moral philosophy and conservative political implications. As philanthropic practice, however, it has been seldom studied. In this paper, we argue that claims to technoscientific expertise are central to how EA actors understand, legitimize, and take part in the production of philanthropic value. We analyze their practices of categorization, ranking and measurement as well as underlying technoscientific imaginaries and moral views through comparing three areas of EA intervention: neglected tropical diseases, cultured meat, and AI safety. We show how EA involves various and contested ambitions to direct knowledge production and redraw the boundaries of expert communities, shedding light on the centrality of technoscience in philanthropists' worldmaking ambitions.

title: Shaping Society's Character: The Role of Schools in Developing Social and Emotional Skills
abstract: This chapter examines how schools cultivate socio-emotional skills that influence both individual success and broader social cohesion. Moving beyond the traditional focus on cognitive ability, I argue that education plays a crucial role in fostering traits that promote cooperation, trust, and long-term societal well-being. Drawing on insights from neuroscience, psychology, and economics, I explore how schools shape not only academic and labor market outcomes but also intergenerational beliefs, attitudes, and the formation of social capital. Using evidence from experimental studies, I highlight how school-based interventions can instill perseverance, enhance social learning, and create environments that curb anti-social tendencies, promote prosocial behavior—ultimately influencing the cultural fabric of society. This perspective reframes education as a mechanism for building more equitable and cohesive communities. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Narrative group intervention for wellbeing and violence reduction among incarcerated women: a Sicilian qualitative study.
abstract: This study describes an action research intervention conducted in the female ward of a Sicilian penitentiary, aimed at promoting emotional awareness, enhancing relational competencies, and fostering solidarity, with the consequent goals of reducing interpersonal violence and improving psychological wellbeing. The intervention involved 20 women over one month, employing female Greek myths as narrative tools to facilitate the elaboration of traumatic experiences and the reconstruction of personal identity. Two groups of ten participants engaged in one two-hour session per week for each group over four consecutive weeks (totaling 4 sessions / 8 h per participant). Needs assessment was conducted through individual clinical interviews. The intervention produced heightened awareness of experienced violence, improved emotional regulation, and strengthened metacognitive capacities. Participants spontaneously assumed the role of peer educators, disseminating content throughout the broader ward community. A marked improvement in the relational climate was observed, alongside emerging solidarity dynamics. Artistic artefacts served as instruments of public representation and institutional communication. The absence of a control group, ethically precluded in custodial settings, restricts causal inference. Outcome assessment relied primarily on qualitative observation rather than standardised psychometric instruments. Penitentiary contingencies prevented follow-up evaluation of the stability of observed changes. Findings pertain to a single Sicilian institution and may not be generalisable across diverse custodial contexts. Future research should incorporate pre- and post-intervention standardised measures, longitudinal follow-up, and comparative analysis of different narrative typologies to strengthen evidence and enhance replicability of the intervention model. The intervention demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of myth-based narrative group work in women's custodial settings, providing practitioners with a structured, gender-sensitive and culturally accessible psychoeducational model. The protocol - characterised by brief duration, low resource requirements, and adaptability to varied educational levels - is transferable across different institutional contexts. The spontaneous emergence of peer education dynamics further suggests that structured group interventions can amplify their impact beyond formal participants. Penitentiary professionals, psychologists and educators may adopt and adapt this approach to promote emotional regulation and violence reduction. This study contributes to advancing gender-responsive and rehabilitative approaches within the penitentiary system, addressing the specific vulnerabilities of women in prison. By targeting interpersonal violence and promoting prosocial dynamics, the intervention supports safer detention environments and broader social reintegration. The emphasis on solidarity, emotional competence and identity reconstruction speaks to wider societal commitments to gender equality, restorative justice and the reduction of social inequalities. The cascading effects observed through peer education indicate potential for sustainable, community-level change within custodial institutions, with implications for public health and post-release social inclusion. This study makes an original contribution by introducing female Greek myths as narrative mediators in a women's prison psychoeducational intervention, demonstrating their effectiveness across diverse educational levels without requiring direct trauma exposure. A further distinctive element is the spontaneous emergence of peer education dynamics, indicating the capacity of structured group work to generate systemic change beyond formal boundaries. The interdisciplinary integration of anthropological and psychological perspectives, combined with an ecologically situated action research design, provides a novel and transferable framework for evidence-informed practice in custodial settings. title: Postnatal mothers’ knowledge, perceptions and sociocultural influences on donor human milk acceptance in Richards Bay, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
abstract: Background Donor human milk (DHM) is a critical alternative for vulnerable infants when maternal milk is unavailable, but its clinical utilisation in South Africa is constrained by limited understanding of how maternal knowledge, perceived safety, cultural meanings and social contexts shape local acceptance. Aim To explore postnatal mothers’ knowledge, perceptions and sociocultural influences shaping acceptance of DHM in Richards Bay, KwaZulu-Natal. Methods A qualitative design informed by interpretive phenomenology was used. Twenty-two postnatal mothers were purposively recruited from a private hospital. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in English or isiZulu, and data were transcribed, translated where necessary, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis supported by reflexivity, peer debriefing, member checking and an audit trail. Results Four themes were developed. DHM was largely unfamiliar, with participants reporting limited prior information and little exposure through routine maternal healthcare. Safety concerns centred on infection, donor health, screening, storage and milk processing, although confidence in healthcare institutions facilitated acceptance for some mothers. Acceptance was also shaped by maternal identity, emotional attachment to breastfeeding, spiritual and cultural beliefs, and family and community influence. Limited awareness did not equate to fixed rejection: after DHM was explained, participants distinguished between receiving and donating: willingness to receive DHM for their own infants was conditional on safety assurance and provider recommendation, whereas willingness to donate was expressed more readily and was often motivated by altruism and reciprocity. These findings indicate an interaction between informational uncertainty, institutional trust, cultural meaning and social legitimacy in shaping DHM decisions. Conclusion Supporting informed decision-making about DHM, and potentially its uptake, requires more than increasing awareness. Routine antenatal and postnatal education, provider training, transparent communication about safety, and culturally responsive family and community engagement may help convert conditional openness into informed acceptance and donation.

title: Family events and child behavior in late childhood: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: Children's social behavior develops through diverse experiences. However, the relationship between children's experiences of celebratory events and their behavioral development has not been previously quantified. Therefore, this study aimed to quantitatively explore this relationship. In 2020, a self-reported questionnaire was completed by 653 sixth-grade students (aged 11-12 years) and/or their caregivers in Nagoya, Aichi, a major metropolitan area in Japan. The main items surveyed were children's experiences with events celebrated by their family and their behavioral development. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire was used to assess children's behavior. This questionnaire identifies behavioral and emotional problems and prosocial behavior. Multiple regression analysis was conducted with the number of family events experienced by children as the explanatory variable and their emotional and prosocial behavior as the objective variables. Children from families who participated in fewer family events tended to have higher problematic behavior risk scores and lower prosociality scores compared with their counterparts. Compared with children who participated in more than 20 family events, those who participated in fewer than 10 family events had more than three times the risk for exhibiting problem behaviors (odds: 3.558, 95% CI: 1.252-10.111, p = .017) and prosocial problems (odds: 3.184, 95% CI: 1.726-5.876, p < .001). Conversely, children from families who participated in more family events tended to have lower problematic behavior risk scores and higher prosociality scores. A higher number of family events may reduce the risk of behavioral problems in children and increase their prosociality. Enjoying family events may be beneficial for social adjustment.

title: Exploring Donor Giving, Intent, and Expectations of Disaster Relief Nonprofits: The Kangaroo Island Bushfire Case
abstract: ABSTRACT In response to concerns regarding how disaster relief nonprofit organizations distribute financial donations, this paper explores individual donor giving, intent upon giving, and expectations subsequent to giving, in the context of the 2019/20 Kangaroo Island bushfires in South Australia. Adopting fundamental constructs from the theory of planned behavior, we examine why people give to natural disaster fundraising campaigns. We then compare donor intent and their expectations of nonprofits subsequent to giving, with nonprofits' actions and communication to consider how (un/met) expectations might impact on attitudes to future giving. A qualitative approach was adopted involving 14 semi‐structured interviews with individual donors (most of whom were geographically close to the disaster location), publicly available communication regarding the disaster, and e‐mail correspondence with the relevant nonprofits. Findings reveal the importance of closeness (geographical, emotional and psychological) to a range of factors influencing giving behavior. Contrary to extant literature that cautions a misalignment between donors' intent, expectations, and nonprofits' actions, this occurrence did not impact negatively on donors' satisfaction or attitudes towards future giving behavior. Implications extend to better understanding why donors give, their expectations following a natural disaster, and the multiple dimensions of donor closeness.
